title: Unprotected admin-ajax Handlers Registered on wp_ajax_nopriv_

rules.description: Handler registered on wp_ajax_nopriv_ — reachable by anyone on the internet
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches the quoted hook string wherever it appears, which is deliberate: it fires on the plain add_action( 'wp_ajax_nopriv_x', ... ) form, on concatenation ( 'wp_ajax_nopriv_' . $action ), on interpolation ( "wp_ajax_nopriv_$actionName" ), and on wrapper APIs such as $this->loader->add_action(...) and a plugin's own loader->my_add_action(...) that a rule anchored on ^\s*add_action would miss entirely. A hit is not automatically a vulnerability — some endpoints are legitimately public (a search suggest, a public form submit, a payment webhook) — but each one is an unauthenticated entry point that must be justified. The volume is low enough to enumerate every hit by hand in any plugin.

rules.description: AJAX hook name assembled from a bare prefix — the action name is not greppable
rules.false_positive_notes: Catches add_action( 'wp_ajax_' . $action, ... ) and add_action( 'wp_ajax' . $x, ... ), where the registered action name exists only at runtime. Benign as a construct, but it means the endpoint inventory cannot be completed by grepping action names — you must read what feeds the variable, which is usually a route table, a $_REQUEST value, or a loop over a class's public methods. The _nopriv_ variant of this shape is already covered by AJAX-001; this rule exists to stop the inventory silently coming up short.

rules.description: Every AJAX registration — the full endpoint inventory, including Subscriber-reachable ones
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately a superset of AJAX-001: it also matches the wp_ajax_ (logged-in) twin. That is the point. wp_ajax_{action} authenticates but does not authorize — it admits every Subscriber, which on a site with open registration, WooCommerce customers, LMS students or forum members is effectively the internet plus one signup form. Use this rule to build the inventory, then diff it against current_user_can() occurrences. Does not match the bare string 'wp_ajax' or admin_url('admin-ajax.php'), so it stays usable.

rules.description: admin-post handler registered for logged-out callers
rules.false_positive_notes: Same trust model as wp_ajax_nopriv_ and worth a separate rule because admin-post.php is designed for form submissions that perform a state change and redirect, so its handlers are far more likely to write than to read. Note it also matches the bare 'admin_post_nopriv' hook (no action suffix), which fires when $_REQUEST['action'] is EMPTY — an easy endpoint to miss when enumerating by action name.

rules.description: A nonce published into a page, i.e. readable by whoever can load that page
rules.false_positive_notes: Publishing a nonce to the page is how AJAX is supposed to work, so most hits are normal. The rule matters because a nonce is routinely the ONLY control on a nopriv handler, and then the real question is who can read it. Follow each hit to its wp_localize_script() / wp_add_inline_script() call and to the enqueue hook: wp_enqueue_scripts means every anonymous visitor, and an unconditional admin_enqueue_scripts means every logged-in user including Subscribers. Either way the nonce is not an access control.

rules.description: Variable dispatch inside a handler — the sink is not statically reachable from the hook
rules.false_positive_notes: Reclassified low by scripts/test_rules.py: this fires on correct code in tests/fixtures/safe.php, and kb/SCHEMA.md reserves high/medium for rules that stay silent there. No coverage is lost - the high-confidence rules in this class still cover the unambiguous shapes; this one is the worklist that needs triage. Common in framework code and often benign. It becomes critical when the dispatching function is a nopriv handler: one registration then exposes every method of the target class, and no sink-side rule can connect the hook to the sink because the edge does not exist until runtime. Whenever a hit sits inside an AJAX-001 handler, enumerate the full set of methods that can be selected and rate the worst one.

rules.description: Ajax-context predicate used as an authorization guard
rules.false_positive_notes: wp_doing_ajax() and DOING_AJAX answer "did this request come through admin-ajax.php". They are true for a completely anonymous request and carry no authorization value at all. Legitimate uses exist — suppressing output buffering, choosing a response format, skipping a redirect — so read the guarded block. If it writes anything, it is a finding. The same reasoning applies to is_admin(), which is covered by WP-AUTHZ AUTHZ-004.

title: Authentication bypass — the login decision itself is wrong

rules.description: The account to authenticate as is named by the request
rules.false_positive_notes: There is no benign form. Casting with absint()/intval() on the same line does not help — it produces a valid user ID, and user ID 1 is the original administrator on almost every install. The only safe sources for this argument are get_current_user_id() or an ID derived from a credential the server has just verified.

rules.description: Loose comparison of an OTP, token, secret or signature
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches both operand orders and is written so that === and !== cannot match: the first branch requires a non-'=' character after the operator, and the second requires a non-operator character before it. Two distinct exploits fall out of a loose comparison here — PHP 8 compares a string against a bool by casting the string, so any non-empty stored secret equals true; and an absent value read back as '' equals an empty submitted value. Neither requires knowing the secret. The correct form is hash_equals().

rules.description: Identity taken from a cookie
rules.false_positive_notes: A cookie is request data with better manners; it is set by the client and can be set to anything. The false positives are cookies whose name merely contains one of the keywords without carrying identity (a login_redirect_url, a user_locale preference), so read what the value is used for. The finding is a cookie value that selects WHICH account a flow operates on — especially as a fallback when a provider omits an email address.

rules.description: A value normalised to an int before its error state is checked — absint( WP_Error ) is 1
rules.false_positive_notes: `$user_id = absint( $user_id );` is idiomatic and usually harmless. It is a critical bug when $user_id holds the return of wp_insert_user()/wp_update_user()/wp_authenticate(), because casting a WP_Error object to int yields 1 — the original administrator — and any subsequent is_wp_error() check can then never fire. Establish what the variable held before the cast; validate first, normalise second.

rules.description: Authentication token or OTP generated from a predictable source
rules.false_positive_notes: rand()/mt_rand() are not cryptographically secure, uniqid() is derived from the clock, and time() is fully known to the attacker. Hashing the output does not add entropy. Also grade the search space independently of the source: a six-digit numeric OTP is 10^6 candidates and is only safe behind strict rate limiting that this rule cannot see. Correct alternatives are random_bytes(), wp_generate_password() and wp_generate_uuid4().

rules.description: Plugin overriding a core authentication decision through a filter
rules.false_positive_notes: Legitimate for SSO, API-key and app-password integrations, so hits need reading rather than reporting. These filters ARE the login decision: returning a user object from determine_current_user authenticates that user for the whole request, and returning true from rest_authentication_errors short-circuits core's REST nonce check in rest_cookie_check_errors(). Check the failure path (does it return null on error, or something truthy) and the scope (does the filter apply to every request or only the plugin's own routes).

rules.description: Anonymous AJAX route on a login-shaped action
rules.false_positive_notes: A login endpoint must be anonymous, so this is a reachability signal rather than a defect. It matters because it enumerates the exact handlers where AUTHBYPASS-001 through -005 apply. Treat any nopriv handler that reaches a login sink as in scope for full manual review, and remember that a nonce on such a handler is not an authorization control.

rules.description: Hash or signature compared with a loose operator instead of hash_equals()
rules.false_positive_notes: Two problems in one shape. The comparison is not constant-time, and with == PHP's numeric string juggling historically made distinct hashes compare equal (the "0e" magic-hash case) — still worth flagging because the same code is often ported to contexts where it applies. strcmp() compared loosely against 0 additionally treats a null return (non-string argument) as a match. Replace with hash_equals().

rules.description: Every login sink — the exhaustive worklist
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches correct code by design, and the list is short in almost every plugin — which makes exhaustive manual triage the recommended workflow for this class. For each hit, walk backwards and answer one question: what fact did the server establish, using data the attacker cannot control, that justifies logging in as THIS account? If the answer involves a value that arrived in the request, the finding is here.

title: Missing or Insufficient Capability Check on a Privileged Handler

rules.description: A role name passed to current_user_can() where a capability belongs
rules.false_positive_notes: Almost never intentional. It happens to work on a default install because the wp_capabilities usermeta array literally contains administrator => true, so that key lands in $user->allcaps. It breaks the moment a membership, LMS or e-commerce plugin renames the role, clones it, or grants the same powers to a different role — and it is silently false for a Super Admin on multisite who holds no site role at all. WPCS flags this as WordPress.WP.Capabilities RoleFound. Fix by naming the capability the action actually needs.

rules.description: Meta capability checked with no object ID — fail-closed on WP 6.1+, wrong-object below
rules.false_positive_notes: The closing paren immediately after the string is the whole signal, so this does not match the correct current_user_can( 'edit_post', $post_id ) form. Two different bugs share the shape. For post/term/comment caps, WP >= 6.1 appends do_not_allow and the check returns false for everyone including Super Admins — a broken feature, not an escalation, and invisible in production because _doing_it_wrong() is silent without WP_DEBUG. For the USER caps (edit_user, delete_user, promote_user, remove_user) there is no such guard: they fall through to the primitive (edit_users, delete_users, promote_users, remove_users), which silently drops the per-object protections — that variant IS an escalation. Read capability-matrix.md §4 before rating.

rules.description: Role membership or legacy user level tested instead of a capability
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches role names used in non-authorization contexts too — a label array, a get_users( array( 'role__in' => ... ) ) query, a settings dropdown. Read the line. It is a finding when the result gates an action. user_level and level_N have been deprecated since WP 3.0 and are not maintained; a plugin that adds capabilities to a role does not change its level, so a level check is stale by construction.

rules.description: A non-authorization predicate used as the guard on a state change
rules.false_positive_notes: is_admin() is legitimate for deciding WHAT TO LOAD ("only register this menu on admin screens") and that use is common, so expect benign hits. It is never an authorization check: admin-ajax.php and admin-post.php both define WP_ADMIN = true before any login check, so is_admin() is true for a fully anonymous request (see entry-points.md §1). is_user_logged_in() is a real but very weak gate — it admits every Subscriber, and on a site with open registration or WooCommerce customers that is effectively the whole internet plus one signup. Rule: if the guarded block writes anything, this is a finding.

rules.description: Capability supplied as a variable, filter, option or constant rather than a literal
rules.false_positive_notes: Legitimate in generic framework code that receives the capability from a caller which hard-codes it. It becomes a finding when the value is reachable from configuration — $this->capability defaulting to 'read', a settings field, or an apply_filters() hook any other plugin can lower. Trace the default. A default of 'read', 'exist' or 'level_0' means every logged-in user passes.

rules.description: A site-takeover-critical option written from plugin code
rules.false_positive_notes: A plugin has almost no legitimate reason to write these. default_role plus users_can_register is the anonymous-administrator pair (capability-matrix.md §6.8); wp_user_roles rewrites the whole role table; siteurl/home enable a persistent redirect and script-source hijack; admin_email/new_admin_email redirect password recovery. If any of these is written, the handler needs manage_options AND a nonce, with no exceptions.

rules.description: Option or metadata write whose KEY is not a literal — an arbitrary-write primitive
rules.false_positive_notes: High volume: a computed key like $this->prefix . '_settings' matches and is usually fine. The question to answer for each hit is whether the key can be influenced by the request. If it can, the handler is an arbitrary-option-write or arbitrary-usermeta-write primitive, and per capability-matrix.md §6.8 that is Critical regardless of what the developer thought they were storing — because default_role, users_can_register and wp_capabilities are reachable through it.

rules.description: State-changing sink fed directly by a request superglobal on the same statement
rules.false_positive_notes: This is the closest a line-oriented rule gets to the actual bug, because a write driven straight off a superglobal is a request handler by definition — so the enclosing function is exactly the one that must contain a capability check. A hit is NOT itself a finding: read upward to the top of the function and to the add_action() that registers it. Misses every multi-line case ($x = $_POST['x']; ... update_option( 'k', $x );), which is the majority; pair it with AUTHZ-007 and AUTHZ-009.

rules.description: Privilege-granting sinks — the worklist that must never be reachable without a capability check
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately a worklist, not a verdict. Registration plugins call wp_insert_user() legitimately; membership plugins call set_role() legitimately. The rule's value is completeness: every one of these sinks grants privilege, so for each hit the auditor must answer three questions — which hook reaches this function, does that function call current_user_can() before the sink, and does the failure branch actually terminate. wp_set_auth_cookie() and wp_set_current_user() deserve special attention: they issue or assume an identity, so reaching either from a request-controlled user ID is authentication bypass, not merely missing authorization.

title: Missing or incorrect nonce verification (Cross-Site Request Forgery)

rules.description: Nonce verification gated on the presence of the nonce field — omit the field and the check is skipped
rules.false_positive_notes: The safe idiom is negated — `if ( ! isset( $_POST['_wpnonce'] ) || ! wp_verify_nonce( ... ) )` — and this rule deliberately does not match it, because the leading `!` is what makes the absent-nonce case fail closed. A positive `isset()` wrapping the verification means the attacker chooses whether the check runs at all. The residual false positive is `if ( isset( $_POST['_wpnonce'] ) && wp_verify_nonce( ... ) ) { ...work... }` where the work is inside the block; read the block boundary before dismissing a hit.

rules.description: Bare wp_verify_nonce() statement — the boolean result is computed and thrown away
rules.false_positive_notes: Essentially always a finding. wp_verify_nonce() is the only one of the three verification helpers that RETURNS instead of terminating, so a statement-position call does nothing at all. check_admin_referer() and check_ajax_referer() call wp_die() themselves, so a bare statement is their correct usage — that is why they are excluded here and handled by CSRF-003/CSRF-009. The `@?` prefix is present for the same reason as in WP-DELETE: suppressed calls occur.

rules.description: check_ajax_referer() with $die=false whose boolean result is discarded
rules.false_positive_notes: Passing false as the third argument converts check_ajax_referer() from a terminating guard into a predicate. Ending the statement there discards the predicate. Rare but unambiguous; the only benign shape is `$ok = check_ajax_referer( 'a', 'n', false );` which this does not match because of the trailing `;` immediately after the closing paren.

rules.description: wp_verify_nonce() called with a single argument — no $action, so it verifies against -1
rules.false_positive_notes: $action defaults to -1, so the token is verified against a generic action any page on the site can mint. Deliberately narrowed to a bare superglobal argument so that the balanced-paren case `wp_verify_nonce( sanitize_text_field( wp_unslash( $_POST['n'] ) ), 'act' )` cannot be mistaken for a one-argument call; the cost is that a single-argument call through an intermediate variable is missed. Pair with CSRF-009 when auditing exhaustively.

rules.description: Inverted nonce guard on one line — a VALID nonce takes the early-return branch
rules.false_positive_notes: Only matches the non-negated form, so the correct `if ( ! wp_verify_nonce( ... ) ) { return; }` never fires. Line-oriented: it misses the (more common) shape where the brace opens on the `if` line and `return false;` sits on the next line. When triaging a hit from CSRF-004 or CSRF-009, read two lines further and check the polarity by hand.

rules.description: REST route registered with no intent check — permission_callback always returns true
rules.false_positive_notes: Legitimate on a genuinely public read-only route (a public search endpoint). On anything that writes, it is a finding: `permission_callback` is the ONLY place a REST route can express an authorization decision, and returning true unconditionally also removes the route from the set of things core will refuse. Grade by the HTTP method and by what the callback does, not by whether the callback contains a `current_user_can()`.

rules.description: Nonce minted into front-end JavaScript, making it obtainable by any anonymous visitor
rules.false_positive_notes: Not a vulnerability by itself — this is how every legitimate AJAX form works. It matters as the second half of a pair: when a handler's only control is a nonce, this rule tells you whether an attacker can simply fetch the nonce. Check which enqueue hook the surrounding wp_localize_script()/wp_add_inline_script() runs on. `wp_enqueue_scripts` (front end) means anonymous; `admin_enqueue_scripts` means logged-in-with-that-screen.

rules.description: HTTP Referer used as the CSRF control
rules.false_positive_notes: Often benign (redirect-back-to-previous-page). It is a finding when the value gates a state-changing branch: Referer is attacker-influenced, frequently absent under privacy settings and referrer-policy headers, and the "absent" case is usually coded as allow. Distinguish from core's wp_get_referer()/check_admin_referer(), which combine the referer with a real nonce.

rules.description: Every nonce verification site — the exhaustive worklist
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches correct code by design; the point is completeness. Most plugins have few enough of these to triage by hand. For each hit ask three questions in order: (1) is the result acted on, (2) is the $action string specific to this operation rather than shared across the plugin, (3) is there a current_user_can() alongside it. A "no" to (3) is not a CSRF finding — it is a WP-AUTHZ finding, and the two are frequently present together.

title: Formula (CSV) Injection in exported data
fix_apis: Prefix the field with a single quote or a space when it begins with = + - @
str_replace() to strip tab and carriage return from exported fields

rules.description: Any fputcsv() call — the exhaustive worklist of CSV emit sites
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches correct code by design; the point is completeness. Plugins have few CSV emit sites, so reading every hit is cheap. For each one ask: does any field originate from a request, a form submission, a comment, a username, or a search query, and is each field neutralised before it is written? A field that only ever holds an integer, a timestamp, or a value the plugin generated itself is not a finding.

rules.description: A whole row variable written straight to fputcsv() with no per-field neutralisation
rules.false_positive_notes: This is the exact shape of CVE-2024-3214: `fputcsv( $df, $row )` inside a foreach over rows read back from the database. It is safe only if the fields were neutralised earlier — commonly by an array_map() a few lines above, or at write time before storage. Read upward for that. Neutralising at write time is a legitimate strategy but a fragile one: it protects only rows written after the fix shipped, so check whether existing stored rows were backfilled.

rules.description: A CSV download endpoint — Content-Disposition attachment with a .csv filename
rules.false_positive_notes: Fires on every CSV export, correct or not. Its value is locating the export endpoints so the two questions can be asked: who may call this (an unauthenticated export is how the highest-scoring CVEs in this class arise), and is each field neutralised. Pair each hit with the nearest capability and nonce check.

rules.description: Hand-rolled CSV assembled by joining fields with commas, bypassing fputcsv() entirely
rules.false_positive_notes: Comma-joining is ubiquitous in PHP for building SQL fragments, class attributes and display strings, so most hits are unrelated. It is a finding only when the result is written to a file or an attachment response. Confirm by looking for a nearby Content-Disposition header or a file write. Hand-rolled CSV also usually gets quoting wrong independently of formula injection.

rules.description: Incomplete formula-character guard — checks some of = + - @ but not all of them
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches a guard whose denylist holds exactly ONE formula character. The complete set Excel, LibreOffice and Google Sheets treat as formula starters is = + - @, plus tab and carriage return, which are handled separately. A guard that stops `=` and lets `+` through stops nothing: `+1+1` and `@SUM(1+1)` both execute. The complete five-element form used in the CVE-2024-3214 patch does not match this rule.

title: Arbitrary File Deletion via user-controlled path

rules.description: unlink()/wp_delete_file() reached by a request superglobal on the same statement
rules.false_positive_notes: Essentially always a finding. The only safe form is when the superglobal has already been mapped through an allowlist or converted to an integer ID on the same line. Note the leading @? — suppressed unlink() is extremely common in this class because the developer expected failures.

rules.description: unlink()/wp_delete_file() on a concatenated path
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches "$base . $name" and "$this->_root_app . $this->_filename" forms. Triage by establishing the provenance of the right-hand operand. A concatenation means no canonicalisation happened at the call site, so the containment check (if any) must be found and verified upstream.

rules.description: Any deletion sink — full triage worklist
rules.false_positive_notes: Noisy but bounded: most plugins have only a handful. Every hit deserves the question "can the argument be influenced by a request, directly or through stored state?". wp_delete_file() is a thin core wrapper around unlink() and offers no protection — it only fires the wp_delete_file filter.

rules.description: Recursive / filesystem-abstraction deletion
rules.false_positive_notes: $wp_filesystem->delete( $path, true ) removes a directory tree. If $path is influenced by a request, the impact is far worse than a single unlink(). Also covers hand-rolled recursive removers, which usually appear next to an rmdir().

rules.description: Broken containment check — strpos(...) == 0 accepts false
rules.false_positive_notes: PHP returns false when the needle is absent and false == 0 is true, so a loose "path starts with base" guard passes for every path outside the base. Fires on code that already calls realpath() and therefore reads as safe. Does not match the correct === 0 / !== 0 forms.

rules.description: sanitize_text_field()/sanitize_file_name() used as the path control before a delete
rules.false_positive_notes: sanitize_text_field() does not remove ../, / or \. sanitize_file_name() does strip directory separators, but it is frequently applied to one variable while a different, unsanitised variable supplies the directory portion of the same path.

rules.description: Delete handler on an unauthenticated route
rules.false_positive_notes: A delete-shaped handler on an anonymous route is the 9.1 shape. Note that a nonce is NOT an authorization boundary here: in several disclosed cases the required nonce was printed into public page JavaScript or handed out by a separate public endpoint.

rules.description: Path taken from stored state (post meta, option, session) rather than the request
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately broad; use it only when triaging a known deletion sink whose path comes from stored state. The question to answer is whether any endpoint — including a low-privilege or unauthenticated one — can write that meta/option/session key. Several disclosed bugs are exactly this two-step: poison the stored path, then trigger the cleanup routine.

title: Arbitrary File Read / Download — file contents returned to the attacker

rules.description: Content-returning read primitive fed by a request superglobal
rules.false_positive_notes: A hit is a finding unless the argument was mapped through a hard-coded allowlist on the same statement. Overlaps deliberately with WP-LFI's LFI-003: the same tainted value is arbitrary READ through these sinks and remote code execution through include/require, so both classes must fire. Two benign shapes to rule out: the argument is a deliberate remote URL (that is WP-SSRF, a different class), or the handler is a legitimate importer whose input is a just-uploaded temp file. fopen() is included because the read happens later via fgets/fgetcsv/fread — the fopen line is where the path is chosen.

rules.description: Download response headers — enumerate every streaming endpoint
rules.false_positive_notes: Not a vulnerability signature; a complete inventory of the plugin's file-download endpoints, which is almost always a short list. For each one answer: where does the streamed path come from, what capability is required, and is there a realpath() containment check against a canonicalised, trailing-slashed base. Every case study in this class would appear in this inventory.

rules.description: Read primitive on a plain variable — provenance must be traced
rules.false_positive_notes: High volume — every plugin reads its own templates and JSON assets this way. Use it as a worklist and triage by tracing the variable back to its assignment. Prioritise variables named $file, $filepath, $path, $url, $doc, $attachment, $download, $target, and any variable assigned from get_post_meta()/get_option() (see FILEREAD-008) or from a registered query var (FILEREAD-009).

rules.description: basename() applied to the download filename rather than to the read path
rules.false_positive_notes: A specific and instructive shape: the developer calls basename() so the browser gets a tidy filename, and a reviewer reads it as path sanitisation. The variable passed to readfile() a few lines later is still the raw, traversable path. When this rule fires, compare the argument of the Content-Disposition basename() with the argument of the read sink; if they are the same variable and basename() was assigned back to it, the code is fine, and if the basename() result went into a different variable it is not.

rules.description: Non-HTTP exfiltration sinks — files read and shipped elsewhere
rules.false_positive_notes: "Arbitrary file read" does not require readfile(). wp_mail() attachments, ZipArchive builders, CSV/report exporters and WP_Http POST bodies all read a path and deliver the bytes to a destination the attacker may also control. Noisy and worth running anyway, because these sinks are invisible to every rule that looks for a read function. Cross-reference with WP-LFI CVE-2026-5710, where the channel was an email attachment.

rules.description: URL converted to a filesystem path by string replacement
rules.false_positive_notes: The idiom assumes the client-supplied string is one the server previously produced. str_replace() swaps the URL prefix for the directory prefix and leaves everything after it untouched — including ../../.. — so the result is an arbitrary path with a trusted-looking prefix. There is no canonicalisation anywhere in the operation. A hit is a finding unless a realpath() prefix check follows; treat "the URL came from our own page" as an assumption, never a control.

rules.description: Extension or MIME allowlist — confirm it is checked against the string that is opened
rules.false_positive_notes: Extension allowlists are common and usually fine. The failure mode is a DISCREPANCY: the validator derives the extension from one normalisation of the input and the sink opens a different one. Null bytes (validator sees "wp-config.php\0.css", opener truncates at the NUL), URL decoding applied on one side only, double extensions, trailing dots/spaces on Windows, and case folding all produce it. For every hit, find the exact expression the read sink receives and confirm it is byte-identical to the one the allowlist inspected.

rules.description: Path taken from stored state rather than the request
rules.false_positive_notes: The read sink contains no superglobal, so every request-centred rule misses it. Once a download handler is known to read its path from stored state, work backwards: which endpoints can write that meta key or option, and what authorization do THEY require? A Contributor who can set a post meta value owns the download handler's input. Same two-step shape as WP-DELETE's DELETE-008.

rules.description: Registered query vars and rewrite rules — entry points with no superglobal
rules.false_positive_notes: A value registered with add_query_var() arrives from ?name=... exactly like $_GET, but is read as $wp_query->query_vars['name'] or get_query_var('name'), so no superglobal appears anywhere near the sink. Rewrite rules feed the same array. Build the list of registered vars first, then treat every read of one as tainted input. This is the entry point in the Hide My WP Lite case study.

rules.description: URL validator or validate_file() used where a containment check is required
rules.false_positive_notes: Both functions are legitimate and neither is a path control. esc_url_raw() preserves a schemeless absolute path such as /etc/passwd unchanged, because that is a valid root-relative URL. validate_file() returns non-zero for "..", "./" and Windows drive letters, but returns 0 — meaning valid — for any absolute POSIX path. Used together they look like belt and braces and stop neither. A hit matters only when the value goes on to reach a filesystem sink; noisy otherwise.

title: Insecure Direct Object Reference — ownership of the target is never checked

rules.description: Object loaded directly from a request-supplied identifier
rules.false_positive_notes: This is a SUSPICIOUS SINK, not a finding. Loading an object by request id is completely normal — WordPress is built on it. The finding is the ABSENCE of a check, and absence is not greppable. For each hit the triaging agent must answer three questions by reading the enclosing function: (a) is there a current_user_can() naming THIS object id, or an explicit comparison of an owner column against get_current_user_id(); (b) if the object is a post, is its post_status/post_type constrained; (c) is the handler reachable below the privilege the object requires. Note the regex deliberately allows absint()/intval()/(int) between the sink and the superglobal: casting to an integer is input validation and has nothing to do with authorization, and its presence is the most common reason a reviewer marks these lines safe.

rules.description: Write or delete keyed on a request-supplied identifier
rules.false_positive_notes: Higher confidence than IDOR-001 because the impact is a modification rather than a read, and because the core functions listed here do NOT perform capability checks of their own — wp_update_post() and wp_update_user() will happily write to any ID they are given. wp_update_user() with a request-controlled ID and a user_email field is the account-takeover primitive: change the address, then use the normal password-reset flow. Safe only if a per-object capability check on the same id appears above.

rules.description: Custom-table read or write keyed on an id column from the request
rules.false_positive_notes: Plugins that keep bookings, orders, entries, tickets or licences in their own tables get no help from map_meta_cap() — there is no meta capability for a row in wp_myplugin_bookings, so the ownership check must be written by hand and usually is not. A hit is SAFE when the WHERE array also constrains an ownership column, e.g. array( 'id' => $id, 'user_id' => get_current_user_id() ). That single extra pair is the whole fix, and its absence is the whole bug. Read the array, not the call.

rules.description: Singular meta capability invoked without an object id
rules.false_positive_notes: These are META capabilities: they only mean anything when an object id is passed as the second argument, because map_meta_cap() uses the id to decide which primitive to require. Called with one argument they do not fail closed — they fall through to the primitive (edit_post -> edit_posts, delete_user -> delete_users), so the check passes for anyone holding the generic capability and says nothing about THIS object. See kb/reference/capability-matrix.md §4. Near-zero false positives: there is no correct reason to call a singular meta cap without an id.

rules.description: Request parameter that names an object — surface mapping
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately broad and case-tolerant, so it catches order_id, userId, postID, uid and bare id. It also matches words that merely end in "id" (valid, grid, paid) and matches benign ids such as a nonce action id. Its job is to enumerate every request-supplied object reference so each one can be traced to its sink; the value is completeness of the worklist, not precision.

rules.description: REST route whose path contains an object identifier
rules.false_positive_notes: A route of the shape /things/(?P<id>\d+) is an object reference by construction. The question is whether its permission_callback receives $request and checks ownership of THAT id, or whether it only checks a generic capability — the latter is the majority case. Note that a permission_callback which returns a non-boolean falsy value (0, '', array()) GRANTS access; see kb/reference/entry-points.md §5.

rules.description: permission_callback that proves at most that the caller is logged in
rules.false_positive_notes: __return_true is legitimate for a genuinely public, read-only route over public data. is_user_logged_in is legitimate for a route that only ever touches the CURRENT user (and then the handler must use get_current_user_id(), never a request id). Anything else is an IDOR by construction: every Subscriber on the site reaches the handler, and the handler decides which object to act on from the request.

rules.description: Entity array built with a variable ID field
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches the argument arrays passed to wp_update_post()/wp_update_user()/wp_insert_user() even when the request value reached the variable many lines earlier, which is the shape IDOR-002 misses. Deliberately does NOT match 'ID' => get_current_user_id(), which is the safe form. Triage by establishing the provenance of the variable; if it descends from the request, an ownership check must exist between the two.

rules.description: Generic capability used as the only gate on an object-specific action
rules.false_positive_notes: Very common and usually correct — a generic capability is the right gate for a generic action (rendering a screen, listing your own items). It becomes a finding when the handler goes on to act on an id from the request: "may this user edit posts in general" is not "may this user edit post 47". Cross-reference each hit with IDOR-001/002/003 in the same function; a handler that matches both and matches neither IDOR-004-with-id nor IDOR-010 has no object-level authorization at all.

rules.description: Places the code establishes who the caller is — inverse grep
rules.false_positive_notes: Not a vulnerability signature — the opposite. Ownership checks are invisible to pattern matching, but their ABSENCE becomes visible when you list every place the caller's identity is resolved. Run IDOR-001/002/003 to get the sinks, run this to get the identity sites, and treat every sink function that contains no identity site as an unauthenticated-target handler until proven otherwise. Beware hits that only WRITE the identity (update_user_meta( $id, '_author', get_current_user_id() )) without ever reading it back — the WCFM case study is exactly that.

title: Sensitive Information Disclosure

rules.description: Log, backup, dump or export file written to a path under the document root
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches any literal filename with a data extension joined to a webroot-relative base. Many hits are legitimate assets (a bundled .json or .txt). The finding is a file whose CONTENT is sensitive — a debug/payment/API log, a database dump, a backup archive, a CSV export of form entries — sitting anywhere the web server will serve it. The base being wp_upload_dir()['basedir'] is the worst case, because uploads/ is served with directory indexes on many hosts and is never protected by core. Note the regex only sees a literal filename; a name built from variables (the W3TC case study) is missed.

rules.description: Request data dumped with var_dump/print_r/var_export
rules.false_positive_notes: Debug scaffolding left in shipped code. A hit dumps the whole superglobal into the response, which for $_SERVER includes internal paths, and for $_COOKIE includes the victim's session cookies when the handler output is reflected. Practically always a finding; the only benign form is print_r($x, true) captured into a variable that is then discarded, which this regex cannot distinguish — read the surrounding lines.

rules.description: Plugin turns on error display or debug logging
rules.false_positive_notes: A plugin must never enable display_errors or WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY: PHP warnings carry absolute filesystem paths, and a warning raised inside $wpdb can echo the query. WP_DEBUG_LOG=true writes wp-content/debug.log, which is world-readable by default. Occasionally guarded by a "development mode" option, which is a mitigating factor and not a fix — check whether the option is writable from a request.

rules.description: Hardcoded API key, token or secret literal in source
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches OAuth client IDs and public/publishable keys as well as genuine secrets, and matches placeholder strings in documentation blocks. Triage by asking what the value authorises. Remember that anything in a plugin file is readable by every WordPress installation of that plugin, so a "shared" secret compiled into the source is public — this is the CVE-2026-14487 shape referenced in WP-DELETE, where a hardcoded salt made a keyed hash forgeable offline.

rules.description: User records or user meta returned in a JSON response
rules.false_positive_notes: A hit is a finding only if the endpoint is reachable below the privilege that list_users would require, or if it returns fields the caller should not see (user_email, user_login, user_pass hash, user_activation_key). Confirm the registration site: wp_ajax_nopriv_, permission_callback => __return_true, or a shortcode all put this on an anonymous route. Multi-line array construction is common, so this single-line regex misses many real cases.

rules.description: Whole option value returned in a JSON response
rules.false_positive_notes: Settings-dump endpoints are the standard way plugin admin screens hydrate their UI, and the standard way API keys leak: the settings array usually contains the integration credentials next to the display preferences. A hit is a finding if the route is reachable below Administrator, or if no field allowlist is applied before the response is built.

rules.description: Directory listing built from a request-controlled path
rules.false_positive_notes: Enumeration of an arbitrary directory reveals backup names, .sql dumps, private uploads and the plugin/theme inventory used to pick the next exploit. Note this only fires when the superglobal is on the same statement; the common real shape is scandir($path) with $path assigned from $_POST several lines earlier — see the directory-listing case study. Sweep for bare scandir/glob calls separately and trace each argument.

rules.description: Every nonce mint site — determine who can obtain each nonce
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately broad and cheap: most plugins have a handful. The question for each hit is which template, hook or endpoint renders it. A nonce minted inside a wp_head, wp_footer, wp_enqueue_scripts or shortcode callback is handed to every anonymous visitor, which means every handler protected only by check_ajax_referer() against that nonce is effectively unauthenticated. This rule exists to feed that question, not to produce findings on its own.

rules.description: Exception text or database error echoed to the response
rules.false_positive_notes: $wpdb->last_error and mysqli_error() disclose table names, column names and prefix — the reconnaissance a blind SQLi needs. Exception messages from file operations disclose absolute paths. Benign when the message is a plugin-authored string, so read what the exception actually is. error_get_last() after a failed file read reports the open failure including the resolved path, which turns a "no output" arbitrary-read bug into a filesystem oracle.

rules.description: Any debug-dump primitive — worklist
rules.false_positive_notes: Noisy: print_r($x, true) is a legitimate idiom for building log strings. Use it to enumerate, then keep the hits whose output reaches echo/print/wp_send_json or a file under the webroot. phpinfo() is never acceptable in shipped plugin code and any hit on it should be promoted immediately.

rules.description: Superglobal read with an attacker-named key
rules.false_positive_notes: The index is a variable, so the caller chooses WHICH cookie, header, session key or environment variable is read. If that value is then returned or rendered, the endpoint is a universal read primitive over the victim's cookie jar and the server environment — including wordpress_logged_in_* and any secret placed in $_ENV. Benign only when the variable is provably drawn from a hard-coded allowlist on a nearby line.

title: Path Traversal / Local File Inclusion / Arbitrary File Read

rules.description: include/require reached by a request superglobal on the same statement
rules.false_positive_notes: Catches both concatenation (include $dir . $_GET['x'] . '.php') and interpolation (require_once "inc/{$_REQUEST['x']}Fn.php"). Near-zero false positives; a hit is a finding unless the value was already mapped through a hard-coded allowlist array on the same line, which is rare. Also matches $_SERVER, which is worth flagging because HTTP_HOST / PATH_INFO / HTTP_X_* are attacker-controlled too.

rules.description: include/require of a bare variable — source unknown, must be traced
rules.false_positive_notes: Enormous volume; almost every plugin does this legitimately for its own templates. Use it only as a worklist, and triage by tracing the variable's assignment. Prioritise variables named $template, $tpl, $file, $path, $view, $page, $lang, $controller, $task.

rules.description: File-read primitive fed directly by a request superglobal
rules.false_positive_notes: A hit is a finding unless the argument is a URL being fetched deliberately (in which case it is SSRF, a different class) or unless a realpath() containment check appears on an adjacent line. Check both.

rules.description: Request parameter with a path-like name — surface mapping
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately broad. Its job is to enumerate every request parameter that might become a path, so the auditor can follow each one. Most hits are benign; the value is in the completeness of the worklist, not the precision.

rules.description: basename()/wp_basename() applied to request input and treated as the defence
rules.false_positive_notes: basename() strips directory components, so it does stop plain ../ traversal. It does NOT constrain WHICH file inside the base directory is reached, does not stop a leading URL scheme (php://, data://, phar://) when the value later reaches an include/fopen, and is bypassed on Windows by backslash handling in older PHP. Treat basename() alone as insufficient; the containment check is realpath()+prefix.

rules.description: Broken containment check — strpos(...) == 0 accepts false
rules.false_positive_notes: In PHP, strpos() returns false when the needle is absent, and false == 0 is true. A "path must start with base" guard written with loose == therefore passes for every path that is NOT under the base. Does not match the correct === 0 / !== 0 forms. This is the highest-value regex in the class: it fires on code that already calls realpath() and therefore looks safe to a reviewer.

rules.description: Containment check written as strpos(...) !== false — substring, not prefix
rules.false_positive_notes: Common and usually benign. It is a finding only when used as a directory-containment test: "does the resolved path contain the base string anywhere" is satisfied by /tmp/attacker/wp-content/uploads/../../../etc/passwd-style constructions and by any path where the base appears mid-string. Correct form is a strict prefix test.

rules.description: sanitize_text_field()/sanitize_key() used where a path control is required
rules.false_positive_notes: sanitize_text_field() strips tags and control characters. It does NOT remove ../, slashes, or a leading /. sanitize_key() does remove slashes and dots and is a genuine (if crude) control. Read which one is used.

rules.description: Directly-reachable plugin PHP file that bootstraps itself instead of using WordPress
rules.false_positive_notes: Normal in most files. It becomes important when the file also reads $_GET/$_POST at top level and is not guarded by defined('ABSPATH') — that combination is a script an unauthenticated attacker can hit directly by URL, with no WordPress auth in the path. Pair with a check for a missing `if ( ! defined( 'ABSPATH' ) ) exit;` guard.

title: Arbitrary option / settings update leading to site takeover

rules.description: Option NAME taken from the request — the attacker chooses which option is written or deleted
rules.false_positive_notes: Essentially always a finding, and always Critical regardless of what the plugin intended the feature to do, because the reachable set includes default_role, users_can_register, siteurl, active_plugins and upload_path. The [^,;]* is deliberately unable to cross a comma, so the common and safe update_option( 'literal_name', $_POST['value'] ) does not match — the value being attacker-controlled is a different, far less severe problem.

rules.description: Option name supplied by a variable rather than a literal or constant
rules.false_positive_notes: Fires on the correct allowlisted form `foreach ( $allowed as $key ) { update_option( $key, ... ) }` as well as on the vulnerable one, because the difference is the provenance of the variable and a regex cannot see it. Triage by walking back to where the variable is set: a hardcoded array is safe, a request value or a stored configuration list is not. Catches the static-wrapper form (`Option::update_option( $k, $v )`) that OPTIONS-001 misses.

rules.description: Settings import / restore / migrate entry point — bulk option writes with a single authorization decision
rules.false_positive_notes: Names a function, not a defect. These handlers are over-represented in this class because one weak check governs an unbounded number of option writes, and because the payload is usually a JSON or serialized blob whose keys nobody enumerates. For each hit, find the authorization check and then find the key allowlist; the allowlist is usually absent.

rules.description: Option names that convert an arbitrary write into full takeover — use to grade an OPTIONS-001/002 hit
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches reads as well as writes, and legitimate plugins do read siteurl/admin_email/ active_plugins. The rule is a severity oracle, not a vulnerability detector: when an OPTIONS-001 or OPTIONS-002 hit has no key allowlist, every name on this list is reachable and the finding is Critical. A hit in isolation only tells you the plugin touches a security-relevant option — check whether it also WRITES it and under what guard.

rules.description: Anonymous AJAX route on a settings-shaped action name
rules.false_positive_notes: A settings writer registered for anonymous callers is the 9.8 shape. Some hits are benign (a nopriv 'save_contact_form' that writes a post, not an option). Cross-reference with OPTIONS-007 to see whether an option sink is reachable from the handler, and remember the inverse case: a handler registered ONLY on wp_ajax_ is still reachable by every Subscriber.

rules.description: Authentication standing in for authorization — credentials verified, capability never checked
rules.false_positive_notes: $wp_xmlrpc_server->login() and wp_authenticate() answer "are these credentials valid", which every Subscriber's credentials are. XML-RPC method handlers are the classic case because the login() call at the top of every method reads like a gate. Legitimate hits exist in genuine login flows; the finding is a login() call followed by a privileged operation with no current_user_can() between them.

rules.description: Every option write or delete — the exhaustive worklist
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches correct code by design. Most plugins have a manageable number of these. For each hit answer: is the option NAME fixed in code; is there a current_user_can( 'manage_options' ) on the path; and is there a nonce. Note that this rule cannot see plugin-level wrappers (Options_Service::update_options(), $this->settings->save(), Carbon Fields, CMB2, ACF option pages) — find those wrappers by name and re-run the same three questions.

rules.description: Option written from a decoded blob, so the key set is defined by the attacker's payload
rules.false_positive_notes: Round-tripping a plugin's own stored JSON is legitimate; decoding a request body into an option is not. Where the blob is unserialize()d rather than json_decode()d the finding is also a WP-POI candidate. base64 in this position is a strong signal the payload was shaped to survive transport, i.e. that it is externally supplied.

title: PHP Object Injection via unserialize() on attacker-influenced data

rules.description: Any call to unserialize() (optionally @-suppressed). In a WordPress plugin/theme codebase this function name is almost never a false alarm — it has no safe idiomatic use that json_decode() would not cover.
rules.false_positive_notes: Tightened after integration testing so the safe two-argument form is no longer matched: the pattern now requires a single argument (no comma before the closing paren), which keeps every true positive including nested decoders. Previously it also matched the safe two-argument form unserialize($d, ['allowed_classes' => false]) and matches function/method *declarations* named unserialize(). Rust-regex has no lookahead, so the allowed_classes exclusion cannot live in the pattern — post-filter hits whose line also contains "allowed_classes". A wrapper method named unserialize() is itself worth reading: wrappers are the single most common way the real sink gets hidden from a grep-based reviewer.

rules.description: Request superglobal flowing directly into unserialize()/maybe_unserialize(), optionally through base64_decode/stripslashes/wp_unslash.
rules.false_positive_notes: Essentially none. Every hit is a real object-injection sink; only the reachability (which hook, which capability check) is in question.

rules.description: maybe_unserialize() applied to a value read back out of the database or a plugin row object — the "round trip" variant where the attacker writes the value first and triggers deserialization later.
rules.false_positive_notes: Safe when the stored value can only ever be written by trusted code. Triage by finding the write side: if any request path (profile field, form submission, import, REST route) can put a string into that option/meta/column, the read side is a live sink. get_option/get_post_meta already auto-unserialize, so an explicit maybe_unserialize on their result usually signals a value that was serialize()d twice — a strong hint the data is user-supplied.

rules.description: PHAR deserialization bridge — a filesystem function taking a request-controlled path. Any stream-wrapper-aware file op on a phar:// path deserializes the archive metadata with no unserialize() call in sight (PHP < 8.0 unconditionally; PHP >= 8.0 still exposes it where the file is opened as a phar).
rules.false_positive_notes: Overlaps with path-traversal and arbitrary-file-read findings; a hit is only a POI issue if the attacker can also plant a .phar (or a polyglot GIF/JPEG containing a phar) somewhere readable — which an upload endpoint usually provides. Flag, do not auto-classify.

title: Privilege escalation via role, capability and account manipulation

rules.description: Role name taken from the request and handed to a user-creation or user-update call
rules.false_positive_notes: Near-zero false positives. wp_insert_user()/wp_update_user() apply NO capability check to the 'role' key — core simply calls WP_User::set_role() with whatever it is given — so a request-supplied role is an unconditional finding unless an allowlist intercepts the value before this line. Note that a sanitiser on the same line (sanitize_text_field, sanitize_key) is not an allowlist: 'administrator' survives all of them intact.

rules.description: set_role()/add_role()/add_cap() called with a variable rather than a literal
rules.false_positive_notes: Common in legitimate membership and e-commerce code, so triage by provenance of the variable. WP_User::set_role() performs no authorization of its own; it writes the capabilities meta directly. A get_role( $x ) or role_exists( $x ) guard upstream is NOT sufficient because 'administrator' is a registered role — the guard must be a positive allowlist of roles this feature may assign, plus a promote_users check on the caller.

rules.description: Direct write to the capabilities / user_level meta key
rules.false_positive_notes: Legitimate code has essentially no reason to write this key by hand — set_role()/add_role() exist for it. Covers both the hardcoded 'wp_capabilities' form and the correct-but-still- dangerous $wpdb->prefix . 'capabilities' form. Treat every hit as a role assignment and ask what capability guards it. Also matches the denylist-construction case, which is exactly what PRIVESC-008 wants you to look at.

rules.description: update_user_meta()/add_user_meta() whose META KEY is a variable — the sink that lets an attacker name wp_capabilities
rules.false_positive_notes: The highest-value rule in this class and the noisiest. A variable meta key is only safe if it came from a hardcoded allowlist. Where it is derived from $_POST/$_GET, from an option an attacker can write, or from a loop over a request array, the attacker names the key — and 'wp_capabilities' is a valid key. Trace the second argument to its origin; do not dismiss a hit because the value looks harmless, since the key is the payload.

rules.description: Target user identified by the request in an account-modifying call
rules.false_positive_notes: Changing another account's email address is account takeover even when no role changes, because the attacker then drives core's own password-reset flow. The only safe forms are get_current_user_id() or an ID that has been through an ownership check — current_user_can( 'edit_user', $id ) is NOT such a check when $id is the caller's own.

rules.description: Handler hooked to a user-profile lifecycle action, which any Subscriber can trigger for themselves
rules.false_positive_notes: Not a defect by itself; it is a reachability signal. personal_options_update fires when a user saves their OWN profile, so a Subscriber reaches the callback with a valid nonce that core printed on their own profile page. Any role or capability write inside such a callback must be gated on promote_users, never on edit_user. user_register fires during open registration and is therefore unauthenticated-reachable when users_can_register is on.

rules.description: A capability check that every logged-in or low-privileged user passes
rules.false_positive_notes: Rated low deliberately: these capabilities are correct in most contexts, so the rule fires on correct code (it hits the legitimate current_user_can( 'edit_posts' ) permission_callback in tests/fixtures/safe.php). Use it as a worklist that is only meaningful when cross-referenced with PRIVESC-002/003/004/006 in the same handler. Correct in its own context and catastrophic in a role-writing one. current_user_can( 'edit_user', $user_id ) with $user_id equal to the caller is always true — every user may edit their own profile — so it authorizes nothing about role changes. 'read' is held by every logged-in user; 'edit_posts' is Contributor and up; 'upload_files' is Author and up. Grade each hit against kb/reference/capability-matrix.md §2 "Choosing the right capability".

rules.description: A denylist of protected user fields — check it for case, prefix and multisite evasion
rules.false_positive_notes: A hit means the author knew the key was dangerous and chose a denylist. Denylists in this class fail three ways, all seen in the wild: case (the comparison runs before sanitize_key() lowercases), multisite prefix (blocking wp_capabilities while wp_2_capabilities reaches the same sink on subsite 2), and completeness (blocking wp_capabilities but not wp_user_level, or the reverse). Convert to an allowlist rather than extending the denylist.

rules.description: Password-reset and credential primitives — the exhaustive worklist
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches correct code by design. For each hit establish: which account the operation targets and how that account was chosen; whether the reset token is unpredictable and single-use; and where the resulting link or code is delivered. A reset flow that lets the requester choose the destination address, or that reuses a publicly visible identifier as the token, is account takeover on every account including the administrator's.

title: Remote code execution via eval, dynamic callables and shell commands
fix_apis: a hard-coded dispatch map (array literal of permitted callables)

rules.description: Any call to eval() or assert(). In a WordPress plugin or theme neither has a defensible use: eval() is the language\x27s own code-injection primitive, and assert() executed a string argument as PHP on every version before 8.0. Read every hit.
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches assert() used in its modern, safe expression form (PHP 7+ with zend.assertions off) and matches method declarations or calls named eval()/assert() - `$engine->eval( $tpl )` is a template-engine wrapper, which is itself worth reading because it usually hides the real sink. Also fires on the literal string "eval(" inside JavaScript embedded in a PHP heredoc; confirm the hit is PHP, not an inline <script> block.

rules.description: A request superglobal used directly as the callable argument of a dispatch function, optionally through one wrapping call such as urldecode() or sanitize_text_field().
rules.false_positive_notes: Essentially none as a *finding*. The only ambiguity is reachability - which hook registers the handler and what capability check runs first. Note that array_map/array_filter/array_walk are included because their first argument is a callable exactly as much as call_user_func\x27s is; `array_map( $_GET[\x27f\x27], $items )` is a full arbitrary-function-call primitive.

rules.description: A dispatch function whose callable argument is a variable rather than a literal - the shape that survives after the request value has been copied into a local, a property or an options array.
rules.false_positive_notes: Downgraded to low after integration testing: this fired on the canonical SAFE allowlist dispatch in tests/fixtures/safe.php. No coverage is lost -- RCE-002 (high) already catches the unambiguous case where a superglobal is the callable. This rule is the broader variable-shaped variant and needs assignment tracing, which is a triage step by construction. The safe idiom matches too: `call_user_func( $allowed[ $key ], $data )` where $allowed is a hard-coded map. Triage by finding the assignment of the callable variable. If it traces to a literal array, a class constant or a hook registration it is fine; if it traces to a request parameter, a shortcode attribute, a block attribute, a post meta value or a plugin option, it is a finding. A `function_exists()` or `is_callable()` guard is NOT an allowlist and does not downgrade the finding.

rules.description: Variable variables ($$name) and dynamic property/variable braces (${$key}). Rare, and almost always a sign that a name is being taken from data rather than written by the developer.
rules.false_positive_notes: Legitimate uses exist in old templating and extract()-style code, and `${$var}` also appears in string interpolation contexts where it is inert. Low volume in practice, so read every hit rather than filtering. Frequently found next to extract(), which turns a request array into local variables and is worth grepping for alongside this rule.

rules.description: Variable function invocation - $fn( ... ). The bare-syntax equivalent of call_user_func(), and the form that grep-based reviews miss most often because it contains no function name at all.
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches every closure invocation, which in modern PHP is common: `$callback( $x )` where $callback was assigned a `function () {}` two lines up is entirely safe. Does not match method calls ($obj->m()), static calls (C::m()) or array-element calls ($map[\x27k\x27]()). Triage by locating the assignment: an inline closure or a literal string is fine, anything derived from input is a finding. Expect a high hit count on codebases that use closures heavily; run it after RCE-002 and RCE-003.

rules.description: Any OS command execution primitive. WordPress core never shells out, so a plugin that does is doing something the platform deliberately avoids and every call deserves review regardless of how the argument is built.
rules.false_positive_notes: The word `exec` is a common method name, so `->exec(` and `::exec(` are deliberately excluded by the leading character class; a database or HTTP client wrapper named exec() would otherwise dominate the results. That exclusion means a genuine `$shell->exec( $cmd )` wrapper is missed - see RCE-007 and the guidance below. Also matches availability probes such as `shell_exec( \x27echo test\x27 )`, which are inert but tell you the plugin has a shell path.

rules.description: A shell primitive whose argument list contains a variable - i.e. the command is assembled rather than constant. This is the subset of RCE-006 where injection is actually possible.
rules.false_positive_notes: Cannot see whether the variable was built with escapeshellarg(). A fully escaped command still matches, and a command where eight of nine arguments are escaped also matches - which is the point, because that is the shape of most real command-injection bugs. For each hit, read the construction of the command string argument by argument and identify the one that is not wrapped. Unlike RCE-006 this rule has no leading-character exclusion, so it does catch `$shell->exec( $cmd )` style wrappers.

rules.description: The backtick shell operator - PHP\x27s syntactic shorthand for shell_exec(), with a variable interpolated into it. Contains no function name, so a function-name-based audit will never see it.
rules.false_positive_notes: Backticks appear in SQL identifier quoting inside PHP strings, so a line like $sql = "SELECT \x60{$col}\x60 FROM t" can match. Distinguish by whether the backtick opens a bare expression (shell) or sits inside a quoted string (SQL). The anchor on `=` keeps the volume low; drop it to a bare backtick-plus-variable search if the codebase is small enough to read all the hits.

rules.description: Legacy code-execution constructs - create_function(), and preg_replace() with the /e modifier, which evaluated the replacement string as PHP.
rules.false_positive_notes: The /e branch can misfire on a pattern whose trailing modifier list legitimately contains an `e` that is not the eval modifier - there is no such standard PCRE modifier, so in practice the only misfires come from a delimiter character appearing inside the pattern body. Both constructs are removed from modern PHP (create_function() removed in 8.0, /e removed in 7.0), so a hit means either dead legacy code or a plugin that still targets PHP 5, and both are worth recording.

title: Open Redirect via unvalidated redirect target

rules.description: wp_redirect() with a request superglobal on the same statement
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately does NOT match wp_safe_redirect(), which routes through wp_validate_redirect() and is correct by default. A hit is a finding unless the superglobal only contributes a query-string fragment appended to a hard-coded local base on the same line. $_SERVER is included on purpose: HTTP_REFERER is the classic "send them back where they came from" source and is fully attacker-controlled, and HTTP_HOST is attacker-controlled on most default vhost configurations.

rules.description: header() built from a request superglobal — open redirect and response splitting
rules.false_positive_notes: Broader than redirects on purpose. wp_redirect() runs wp_sanitize_redirect(), which strips %0d/%0a and everything outside a safe character set, so it is CRLF-safe; a raw header() call has neither that protection nor host validation. Hits on Content-Disposition/Content-Type built from request data are also findings (header injection, content-type confusion) — they just belong to a different class. Read which header is being written.

rules.description: URL escaper or decoder used as if it were a redirect validator
rules.false_positive_notes: esc_url()/esc_url_raw()/sanitize_url() normalise a URL and drop disallowed schemes. None of them restricts the destination host, which is the entire point of an open redirect. urldecode() is actively harmful here — it re-introduces characters an upstream filter already removed, and enables double-encoding bypasses. This regex fires on code that looks defended, which is why it is high confidence: in three of the case studies below, the sanitiser is the only thing between $_GET and the Location header.

rules.description: Location header emitted directly, bypassing wp_validate_redirect entirely
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches constant destinations too (header( 'Location: ' . home_url( '/done' ) )), which are safe. The rule is worth running because every raw Location header is outside WordPress's redirect pipeline: no allowed_redirect_hosts check, no wp_sanitize_redirect(), no wp_redirect filter for other plugins to observe. Triage by asking whether any part of the string is dynamic, and prefer converting the call to wp_safe_redirect() even when the current value is constant.

rules.description: allowed_redirect_hosts filtered — the allowlist wp_safe_redirect() depends on
rules.false_positive_notes: Legitimate and common: payment gateways, SSO providers and OAuth flows must add their own host. It is a finding when the callback appends a request-derived value, returns a wildcard, or adds a host the attacker can control content on (a user-content CDN, a shortener). Read the callback body — this filter is global, so widening it here weakens wp_safe_redirect() for core and every other plugin on the site.

rules.description: Redirect-shaped request parameter — surface mapping
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately broad; most hits are benign and some are correct code (a wp_validate_redirect( $_POST['redirect_to'], admin_url() ) call matches this rule and is the recommended pattern). Its job is to enumerate every parameter that could become a Location header so each can be traced. It is the only rule that fires on CVE-2026-1277, where the assignment and the redirect are on different lines.

rules.description: wp_redirect() of a bare variable — provenance must be traced
rules.false_positive_notes: High volume; most plugins redirect to internally-built admin URLs. Excludes wp_safe_redirect() to keep the list workable. This is the worklist rule for stored/indirect open redirects, where the destination arrives from the database, from an option, or from a REST request object rather than from a superglobal — the shape of CVE-2024-8761 and CVE-2025-6238, neither of which any superglobal-anchored rule can see.

rules.description: Weak "is this URL local" test — leading-slash or http-prefix check
rules.false_positive_notes: A leading "/" test is bypassed by "//evil.tld", which browsers treat as protocol-relative and follow off-site; core handles this explicitly by rewriting a leading "//" to "http://" before parsing. A `strpos( $u, 'http' ) === 0` test accepts every absolute URL on the internet and is not a check at all. Occasionally the surrounding code also rejects "//" on an adjacent line, which makes the hit benign — read both lines. Correct form is wp_validate_redirect(), or a strict "starts with / and does not start with //" pair.

rules.description: Redirect-decision filters whose callbacks commonly return request data
rules.false_positive_notes: Registering these filters is entirely normal. The rule exists to build a worklist: the value a login_redirect / logout_redirect callback returns is handed to wp_safe_redirect() by core (safe) or to wp_redirect() by whatever plugin owns the form (not safe), and callbacks routinely do `return $_REQUEST['redirect_to'];`. Read every callback body; the finding is in the callback, not in the registration.

title: REST Routes with a Missing or Non-Authorizing permission_callback

rules.description: permission_callback set to a __return_* helper that PASSES the dispatch test
rules.false_positive_notes: The four listed helpers all satisfy WP_REST_Server::dispatch(), which rejects only on a STRICT false === or null === comparison: __return_zero gives int 0, __return_empty_string gives '', __return_empty_array gives array() — falsy in PHP, but none of them is false or null, so the endpoint executes for anonymous callers. __return_false and __return_null are deliberately excluded because they DENY. A hit is not automatically a vulnerability: a genuinely public read endpoint is supposed to look like this, and core's own docs recommend __return_true for public routes. It is a vulnerability whenever the callback writes, reads non-public data, or trusts a request-supplied identifier.

rules.description: permission_callback that only proves the caller is logged in, or nothing at all
rules.false_positive_notes: is_user_logged_in as a permission callback admits every Subscriber, which on a site with open registration, WooCommerce customers or LMS students is one signup form away from unauthenticated. is_admin is worse than useless: it returns the WP_ADMIN constant and is false on the REST route in the first place, so it fails closed for everyone and the author will "fix" it by switching to __return_true. Neither answers "may this user do this". Legitimate only when the route exposes exactly what any logged-in user may already see and the handler performs its own object-level check.

rules.description: Named permission-callback definitions — read each body
rules.false_positive_notes: This is an inventory rule and it exists because REST-001 has a blind spot that shows up in real CVEs: a callback named check_permission() whose entire body is "return true;" is functionally identical to __return_true and matches none of the string rules. Expect many benign hits in well-written controllers (WP_REST_Controller subclasses define get_items_permissions_check() and friends by convention). Read every body and classify: returns true unconditionally, checks login only, checks a capability that is too low, checks the right capability, or checks the right capability against the object ID.

rules.description: Permission callback gated on a capability EVERY logged-in user holds
rules.false_positive_notes: read, exist and level_0 are held by every account that exists, including a Subscriber created by open registration; 'subscriber' is a role name, not a capability, and is covered here because it appears in the same position. None of them can authorize anything a route does, so a hit is a finding whenever the route is not intended to be readable by every logged-in user. The only benign case is a route deliberately scoped to "any authenticated user", which should say is_user_logged_in() and be reviewed under REST-002 instead. Contributor/Author primitives such as edit_posts are handled separately by REST-008 because they are legitimate on post-scoped routes.

rules.description: Inline closure or arrow function used as the permission callback
rules.false_positive_notes: A worklist rule, and confirmed as such against tests/fixtures/safe.php, where a correct inline permission callback matches it. Neutral as a construct — many correct callbacks are one-line closures. Flagged because the body is on the same or the next line and is therefore cheap to read, and because arrow functions in particular invite the non-boolean return that REST-006 covers (fn( $r ) => get_current_user_id() grants access to anonymous callers). Read every hit; it is a two-second triage per occurrence.

rules.description: Permission callback returning a non-boolean — falsy values other than false/null ALLOW
rules.false_positive_notes: Only a finding when the enclosing function is a permission callback, so pair it with REST-003 and REST-005 and check the line numbers overlap. The rule matters because dispatch rejects on false === $permission || null === $permission and nothing else: get_current_user_id() returns int 0 for an anonymous caller and 0 is neither, so the route executes. The same trap applies to count() returning 0, strpos() returning 0 at offset zero, absint() of a missing parameter, and get_option()/get_user_meta() returning '' when unset. Any permission callback whose final expression is not obviously a bool or a WP_Error is a finding.

rules.description: Every REST route registration — the inventory to diff against permission_callback
rules.false_positive_notes: Pure inventory. Its job is to be counted: since WordPress 5.5, an omitted permission_callback triggers only a silent _doing_it_wrong() notice, the route is still registered, and dispatch skips the authorization block entirely because it is guarded by ! empty( $handler['permission_callback'] ). A route count higher than the permission_callback count therefore means one or more routes are fully public and no string rule will ever find them. Note also that one register_rest_route() call can define several endpoints (an array of method/callback groups), each needing its own permission_callback — count endpoints, not calls.

rules.description: Permission callback gated on a Contributor/Author primitive with no ownership logic
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately low, and verified against tests/fixtures/safe.php where exactly this shape appears as correct code: on a route that operates on the caller's own posts and re-checks with a meta capability plus the object ID, edit_posts is the right gate. It is a finding when the route touches users, options, settings, files, other people's content, or any request-supplied object ID — because these are primitives with no ownership, status or post-type logic whatsoever (capability-matrix.md §4). This rule found CVE-2025-4672, where edit_posts guarded an arbitrary user-meta write; nothing higher-confidence can, because syntactically the code is a correct capability check.

rules.description: Permission callback is an inline closure that unconditionally returns true — semantically identical to __return_true
rules.false_positive_notes: Added after auditing a real plugin that wrote `permission_callback => function () { return true; }` across three lines. That is exactly as open as `permission_callback => __return_true`, but REST-001 only matches the string form, so the route was invisible at default confidence and only REST-005 (low, hidden by default) saw it. Formatting must not decide whether a route is reported, hence multiline: true — the rule is matched against a short joined window. A genuinely public read-only endpoint is a legitimate use of an always-true callback: a front-end search or a public directory. Treat it as a finding whenever the route writes, or when the callback returns anything the site owner would not publish. For a read route, verify what the callback constrains — a query pinned to post_status => publish and an admin-configured post type list is safe; the same route without those returns drafts and private posts to anonymous callers.

title: Hardcoded credentials, exposed secrets and weak randomness

rules.description: Provider-recognisable credential literal in source (AWS, Stripe, Google, Slack, GitHub, SendGrid, Mailgun, PEM private key)
rules.false_positive_notes: Anchored on issuer-defined prefixes and lengths, so it cannot fire on prose or on a field label. The realistic false positives are (a) provider documentation examples pasted into a comment — AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE is AWS's own published sample — and (b) revoked keys left in a fixture. Both still warrant a look: a key in a public plugin ZIP is compromised whether or not it currently works. Note the pattern requires PRIVATE KEY, not PUBLIC KEY; a PEM public key is not a finding. Zero hits across 78k lines of real plugin code in testing.

rules.description: Security-relevant value generated from a non-cryptographic PRNG
