rules.false_positive_notes: rand()/mt_rand() are Mersenne Twister, seeded from a small space and fully reconstructable from a few outputs; uniqid() is the microsecond clock in hex and is guessable to within a few hundred candidates. None is a CSPRNG. The name list includes the generic `key` and `code`, which is where the false positives live — `$cache_key = ... mt_rand()`, `$widget_id`-style uniqueness values and `$key = array_rand( $items )` are harmless. Triage by asking whether the value is ever compared for authentication or emailed to a user. Two hits across 78k lines in testing, both genuine (one is CVE-2025-4607).

rules.description: Hash of a timestamp or a PRNG value used where a secret is expected
rules.false_positive_notes: Hashing does not add entropy. md5( time() ) has at most one candidate per second and an attacker who triggers the generation knows the second. BUT this idiom is also the standard way to build MIME boundaries, temporary filenames, cache-busting strings and dedup keys, and those are harmless. Measured on real plugin code: 10 hits, 2 genuine (CVE-2024-4185, CVE-2024-5149), 8 benign — roughly 20% precision, hence medium. Triage rule: is the output ever used as a credential, an activation link parameter, or a comparison target?

rules.description: Explicit reseeding of the Mersenne Twister
rules.false_positive_notes: PHP seeds mt_rand() from a strong source automatically since PHP 7.1; calling mt_srand() can only make the stream weaker, and seeding it from microtime() (the universal idiom) reduces the whole sequence to about 10^6 candidates. The only legitimate use is deterministic test fixtures — if the file is not a test, it is a finding. Nothing else in this class produces so much impact from one line; one hit across 78k lines in testing, and it was CVE-2026-14495.

rules.description: WordPress salt/key or DB password defined with a literal value
rules.false_positive_notes: This is exactly what a normal wp-config.php looks like, so the rule is meaningless inside a correctly-ignored config file and critical anywhere else. It is a finding when the file is tracked in version control, shipped inside a plugin/theme ZIP, present in a backup that is web-reachable, or when the value is still the installer placeholder ("put your unique phrase here") — which means every auth cookie on the site can be forged. Pair with a check of .gitignore and of what the deployment artifact contains, not just with a grep.

rules.description: Secret-named identifier assigned a long literal string
rules.false_positive_notes: The literal must be 12+ characters with no whitespace, which eliminates almost all English placeholder text ("Enter your password", "Paste your API key here") and all empty defaults. The residual false positive is a long *identifier* constant assigned to a generic name — `$key = 'my_plugin_settings_v2';` or `'api_key' => 'wc_gateway_api_key_field'` — so read the value and ask whether it looks like an option name or like entropy. Measured on real plugin code: 7 hits across 78k lines, all 7 genuine (CVE-2023-3947, CVE-2023-3371, CVE-2024-5810). This is the highest-precision rule in the class; do not weaken it by adding bare `password` to the name list, which would flag every form field on the internet.

rules.description: Request value compared directly against a literal secret
rules.false_positive_notes: Restricted to secret-shaped parameter names so it does not fire on `$_GET['action'] === 'my_plugin_export'`. A hit is an authentication decision made against a value that ships in the plugin ZIP: every installation shares it and anyone can read it. Low recall by design — the far more common shape assigns the literal to a variable first (`$token = '...'; if ( $data['token'] == $token )`), which SEC-006 catches instead. Run both.

rules.description: Secret compared with loose or non-constant-time equality instead of hash_equals()
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches `==`/`!=` and deliberately does NOT match `===`/`!==` (the trailing [^=] excludes them). Two distinct defects hide here: PHP's loose comparison type-juggles numeric-looking strings, so a purely numeric token can match a different numeric token; and byte-by-byte comparison leaks timing. Emptiness checks (`if ( $api_key != '' )`) are the main false positive — 1 of 5 hits in testing. The fix is hash_equals( (string) $expected, (string) $given ).

rules.description: Credential shipped to the browser or into a JSON response
rules.false_positive_notes: Catches the one-statement form where the key name and the emitting call are on the same line. It cannot see the far more common two-step shape — `$accounts = get_option('..._accounts'); wp_send_json_success( $accounts );` — where no credential name appears at the emit site at all; that is exactly CVE-2026-6446 and it must be found by reading the handler. Also flags settings screens that legitimately re-render a saved key into a password field for the administrator who owns it; the finding is when the emitting route has no capability check.

title: SQL Injection via unprepared $wpdb queries

rules.description: A PHP variable interpolated directly into the string literal handed to a raw $wpdb read/write method. The $wpdb-> prefix properties ($wpdb->prefix, $wpdb->posts, $wpdb->users ...) are excluded from the match because they are server configuration, not user input.
rules.false_positive_notes: Safe only when the interpolated variable is a compile-time constant the request cannot reach (a hard-coded table suffix, an allowlisted column). It cannot be made safe by escaping the value beforehand with esc_sql() unless the author also added the surrounding quotes by hand -- see SQLI-009. The rule is line-oriented, so a query built across several lines is invisible to it; SQLI-006 and SQLI-007 exist to cover that case.

rules.description: String concatenation of a variable into a raw $wpdb read/write method call - the `"... WHERE id = " . $x` shape, including the `'".$x."'` form where the author added quotes but no escaping.
rules.false_positive_notes: The $wpdb-> prefix properties are excluded from the match, so the safe idiom `$wpdb->query( "DROP TABLE " . $wpdb->prefix . "x" )` does not fire. What remains as a possible false positive is a class constant or a locally derived literal concatenated in (`" LIMIT " . $this->page_size`). Check what is on the right of the dot: a superglobal, a function argument or a row value is a finding; a value that traces to a literal is not.

rules.description: $wpdb->prepare() called with a single string argument and no substitution arguments. Core raises _doing_it_wrong for this, and it is a reliable tell that the author believes prepare() sanitises an already-built query string rather than performing substitution.
rules.false_positive_notes: A genuinely constant query wrapped in a pointless prepare() is harmless but still wrong; it will be flagged. Read the string: if it contains an interpolated variable the finding is live, if it is fully literal the finding is only a code-quality issue. The variant `$wpdb->prepare( $sql )` where $sql was assembled earlier is NOT caught here - grep separately for `prepare( $` followed by a bare variable.

rules.description: A variable concatenated into the *query string* passed to prepare(). prepare() substitutes placeholders in the string it receives; anything already concatenated into that string is raw SQL by the time prepare() sees it.
rules.false_positive_notes: The common safe form is a pre-built placeholder list - `prepare( "... IN (" . implode( ",", array_fill( 0, count( $ids ), "%d" ) ) . ")", $ids )`. Distinguish by looking at what the concatenated variable holds: a list of %d/%s tokens is the correct fix, a list of values is the bug. Class properties holding table names ($this->table, $this->tb_posts) also match and are usually safe.

rules.description: A placeholder wrapped in quotes or backticks inside prepare(). %s supplies its own single quotes and %i its own backticks, so \x27%s\x27 produces a doubly quoted, corrupt value and \x60%i\x60 is rejected outright by WPCS (QuotedIdentifierPlaceholder).
rules.false_positive_notes: Rare false positives where a literal quote happens to sit next to a placeholder for reasons unrelated to quoting, e.g. `LIKE %s` inside a longer string containing apostrophes. Also flags numbered placeholders written as \x27%1$s\x27, which are a separate trap: core does NOT add quotes to %1$s-style placeholders, so those genuinely need hand-written quotes and are still worth reading.

rules.description: An interpolated variable in identifier position - after FROM, JOIN, ORDER BY or GROUP BY. Identifiers could not be parameterised at all before WP 6.2 and are the single most common reason a developer abandons prepare().
rules.false_positive_notes: Reclassified low by scripts/test_rules.py: this fires on correct code in tests/fixtures/safe.php, and kb/SCHEMA.md reserves high/medium for rules that stay silent there. No coverage is lost - the high-confidence rules in this class still cover the unambiguous shapes; this one is the worklist that needs triage. Noisy by design and the noisiest rule in this class. On a plugin that keeps table names in class properties ("FROM {$this->tb_posts}") it fires on nearly every query, and it also fires on `ORDER BY x {$order}` where $order is a locally derived \x27ASC\x27/\x27DESC\x27. Treat it as a worklist, not a finding list: for each hit, find where the variable is assigned and stop as soon as you reach a literal. The hits that matter are the ones whose variable traces back to $_GET/$_POST, a shortcode attribute, a REST parameter or a stored option.

rules.description: An interpolated variable on the value side of a comparison inside WHERE/AND/OR/SET/HAVING/LIMIT. Matches inside a multi-line heredoc-style query string, which is where SQLI-001 and SQLI-002 go blind. Also matches the quoted form \x27{$var}\x27, which developers frequently believe is safe.
rules.false_positive_notes: Fires on SQL fragments that are never executed (documentation blocks, README samples, .sql migration text embedded in PHP) and on WP_Query/meta_query array code that merely contains the word AND. It cannot tell whether the surrounding statement ends up in $wpdb->prepare(), so correlate hits with the nearest enclosing $wpdb call before judging.

rules.description: An IN() list built by interpolation or concatenation rather than by generating one placeholder per element.
rules.false_positive_notes: Reclassified low by scripts/test_rules.py: this fires on correct code in tests/fixtures/safe.php, and kb/SCHEMA.md reserves high/medium for rules that stay silent there. No coverage is lost - the high-confidence rules in this class still cover the unambiguous shapes; this one is the worklist that needs triage. The *correct* fix also matches: `"... WHERE id IN( {$placeholders} )"` where $placeholders = implode( ",", array_fill( 0, count( $ids ), "%d" ) ) and $ids is passed to prepare() as the argument array. Read one line up. If the interpolated variable holds placeholder tokens the code is right; if it holds values (even esc_sql\x27d or absint\x27d ones) it is a finding, because %i is not permitted inside IN() and an integer cast is the only other thing that closes it.

rules.description: Any use of esc_sql(). Per core, esc_sql() is spot-escaping of last resort - it adds no quotes, offers no identifier protection, and since WP 4.8.3 rewrites % characters, so its output is unsafe to reuse.
rules.false_positive_notes: esc_sql() used on a value that the author then wrapped in literal single quotes inside the query is technically correct, and esc_sql() applied to an array before an insert is common. Both still deserve a read. The two shapes that are always findings are `WHERE x = " . esc_sql( $v )` (no quotes added, so any numeric-context payload walks straight in) and `esc_sql( implode( ",", $ids ) )` (identifier/list context, where escaping does nothing).

title: Server-Side Request Forgery via unvalidated outbound HTTP

rules.description: Non-validating wp_remote_* call with a request superglobal on the same statement
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately does NOT match wp_safe_remote_* — those set reject_unsafe_urls and are validated by core. A hit is a finding unless the superglobal contributes only to the body/headers rather than to the URL (read which argument it lands in), or unless the value is first mapped through a hard-coded host allowlist on the same line. Note that $_SERVER is included: HTTP_HOST, HTTP_REFERER and HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR are attacker-controlled and are routinely concatenated into callback URLs.

rules.description: Core's private-IP protection disabled globally via the http_request_host_is_external filter
rules.false_positive_notes: This filter is the ONLY escape hatch from wp_http_validate_url()'s private-range check, and it is global: registering it turns off loopback/RFC1918 rejection for every wp_safe_remote_* call made by core, by every other plugin, and by every theme on the site for the rest of the request. '__return_true' is unconditionally a finding. The closure form is matched too and must be read — a closure that inspects $host and returns true only for one known internal hostname is legitimate. The array/[$this,...] callback form is deliberately NOT matched, to keep this rule high-confidence; sweep for the bare filter name separately when auditing a plugin end to end.

rules.description: reject_unsafe_urls explicitly switched off in a request args array
rules.false_positive_notes: wp_safe_remote_*() works by setting this key to true; setting it to false converts a "safe" call back into an unvalidated one while leaving the reassuring function name in place. Also matches the $args['reject_unsafe_urls'] = false; assignment form. The only benign hit is a http_request_args filter callback that sets it false for a specific, hard-coded internal URL — verify the URL is not request-derived.

rules.description: PHP-native fetch primitive fed by a request superglobal
rules.false_positive_notes: These functions have no URL validation whatsoever and PHP's stream wrappers make them dual-use: the same call is SSRF for http://, arbitrary file read for a relative path, and object injection for phar://. A hit is a finding; the only question is which of the three classes it belongs to (often all three — see CVE-2023-2249). Overlaps WP-LFI/LFI-003 by design; do not suppress one in favour of the other.

rules.description: Option / meta / transient NAME built from request data — the attacker chooses which stored value is used
rules.false_positive_notes: Extremely common and usually benign (per-form, per-post, per-widget settings keyed by an ID). It becomes a finding when the retrieved value is then used as a URL, a path or a capability: the request controls which stored string is dereferenced, so any option the attacker can also write becomes the request target. Prioritise hits whose key prefix contains url/webhook/endpoint/callback/api/host, and hits that appear inside a wp_remote_*/curl statement (CVE-2026-17123 matches this rule and SSRF-001 on the same line).

rules.description: Outbound HTTP whose target is not a string literal — the full worklist
rules.false_positive_notes: Enormous volume; nearly every plugin builds its API URL from a constant or property. Its job is completeness, not precision: it is the only rule that catches the multi-hop shape where the tainted fragment is concatenated inside a helper (CVE-2026-78003 is invisible to every other rule here and shows up only as `wp_remote_request( $url, $args )`). Triage by tracing the first argument backwards. Misses the case where the first argument starts with a quote and is then concatenated ("https://api/" . $x) — SSRF-001 covers that when $x is a superglobal.

rules.description: URL sanitiser/validator being used where an SSRF control is required
rules.false_positive_notes: esc_url_raw()/sanitize_url() normalise a URL and strip disallowed protocols. They do NOT restrict the host, so http://169.254.169.254/, http://127.0.0.1:6379/ and http://internal-jenkins/ all pass unchanged. filter_var(..., FILTER_VALIDATE_URL) is weaker still. Hits are only findings when the result reaches a fetch sink; a hit followed on the next line by wp_http_validate_url(), a parse_url() host allowlist, or a wp_safe_remote_* call is correct code — the fixed Getwid release matches this rule and is not vulnerable. Expect a high benign rate; the rule earns its place because this exact false defence appears in CVE-2026-6203, CVE-2026-1277 and CVE-2023-1895.

rules.description: URL-shaped request parameter — surface mapping
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately broad. Most hits never reach an outbound request. The value is a complete worklist of parameters that might become one, so each can be traced by hand; in CVE-2024-5021 this is the only rule that fires, because the sink 14 lines later takes a bare variable.

rules.description: TLS certificate verification disabled on an outbound request
rules.false_positive_notes: Not SSRF by itself, but it belongs to the same audit: it makes every outbound request MITM-able, and it is the standard workaround developers reach for when an internal host has a self-signed certificate — which is a strong hint that the code path is pointed at internal infrastructure. Occasionally legitimate in a local-development guard (`if ( WP_DEBUG )`); read the surrounding condition. Always a finding when the request carries an API key or an auth header.

title: Path Traversal in file writes, moves and archive extraction

rules.description: Write, move or directory-creation sink reached by a request superglobal
rules.false_positive_notes: Essentially always a finding. The only safe form is a destination already reduced to a single filename by wp_basename()/sanitize_file_name() and joined to a fixed base on the same statement. Remember that BOTH operands of rename() and copy() matter: traversal in the SOURCE argument moves an arbitrary server file into a directory the attacker can read, which is the CVE-2025-2941 shape. $_FILES is included because a plugin that builds its own destination from $_FILES[...]["name"] has bypassed wp_handle_upload().

rules.description: Archive extraction surface — Zip Slip
rules.false_positive_notes: Entry names inside an archive are attacker-controlled strings and are the classic traversal vector. Core's unzip_file() and ZipArchive::extractTo() do their own normalisation and are the SAFE forms; the dangerous shape is a hand-rolled loop over statIndex()/getNameIndex() that concatenates $entry["name"] onto a destination directory, because that skips every check the library would have made. When this rule fires, look for the loop, not the class. PharData / Phar also deserialise metadata, so a hit there is a WP-POI candidate as well.

rules.description: path_join() — WordPress core function that discards the base for absolute paths
rules.false_positive_notes: path_join( $base, $path ) returns $path UNCHANGED when path_is_absolute( $path ) is true. It is a convenience helper, not a containment function, and its name invites the opposite reading. A hit is a finding when the second argument can be attacker-supplied: passing "/var/www/html" or a Windows drive letter makes the "base" disappear, and any downstream containment test that compares against the joined result then compares against the attacker's own directory. Benign when both arguments are internal.

rules.description: URL converted to a filesystem path by string replacement before a write
rules.false_positive_notes: Swapping a URL prefix for a directory prefix leaves everything after the prefix untouched, including ../../.., and performs no canonicalisation. The code assumes the client returned a URL the server had previously produced; nothing enforces that. A hit is a finding unless a realpath() prefix check against a canonicalised base follows. Shares its shape with WP-FILEREAD's FILEREAD-006 — the difference is only whether the resulting path is opened for reading or for writing.

rules.description: Request parameter with a destination-shaped name — surface mapping
rules.false_positive_notes: Deliberately broad. Its job is to enumerate every request parameter that could become part of a destination path so each can be traced to a sink. Most hits are benign. Pay particular attention when TWO of these appear in the same handler — one supplying the directory and one the filename — because that means the attacker steers the base as well as the leaf, and any allowlist derived from the base is worthless.

rules.description: Non-path sanitiser used as the path control at a write sink
rules.false_positive_notes: sanitize_text_field() strips tags and control characters and leaves ../, / and \ completely intact. esc_url_raw() preserves a root-relative absolute path. wp_unslash() is a slash-removal helper for magic quotes, not a security control. sanitize_key() and sanitize_file_name() DO strip separators and are genuine (if crude) controls — read which one is present. Frequently a sanitiser is applied to the filename while a different, unsanitised variable supplies the directory portion of the same path.

rules.description: Leading-slash stripping used as the traversal defence
rules.false_positive_notes: "Make sure it is not absolute" is a real check and an incomplete one: it does nothing about ../, it is defeated on Windows by a drive letter (C:\) or a backslash, and ltrim($p, "./") applied once still leaves "....//....//" reducible to "../../" by any normaliser that runs afterwards. A hit tells you the developer thought about traversal and stopped early. Also matches benign ltrim() calls on non-path strings, so read the variable.

rules.description: Write or move sink on a bare variable — provenance must be traced
rules.false_positive_notes: The complete worklist of write/move sinks, and in most plugins it is short enough to triage exhaustively — the recommended workflow for this class. For each hit, establish the provenance of every operand, including the base directory, and remember that copy()/rename() have two path arguments and either can be the tainted one. $wp_filesystem->put_contents()/move() are the WP_Filesystem equivalents and provide no validation of their own.

rules.description: Client-supplied upload filename used to build a destination
rules.false_positive_notes: $_FILES[...]["name"] is a raw client-controlled string; PHP does not sanitise it. A hit is benign when the value is only used for display or is passed to wp_handle_upload() / media_handle_upload(), which apply sanitize_file_name() and wp_unique_filename() internally. It is a finding when the plugin concatenates it onto a directory itself — that is the hand-rolled upload path, and it is also the WP-UPLOAD surface, so both classes apply.

title: Arbitrary File Upload leading to Remote Code Execution

rules.description: Raw move_uploaded_file() — bypasses wp_handle_upload()'s core MIME/extension enforcement
rules.false_positive_notes: A plugin has almost no legitimate reason to call this directly. Safe only if the surrounding code ran wp_check_filetype_and_ext() on tmp_name AND rewrote the destination extension from the verified type. An extension allowlist checked before the move is necessary but not sufficient — verify the destination filename is built from the *verified* extension, not from $_FILES['x']['name'].

rules.description: Client-supplied Content-Type ($_FILES[..]['type']) used as a security decision
rules.false_positive_notes: Benign when the value is only stored/logged/echoed. It is a finding whenever it feeds in_array(), a switch, str_starts_with(), strpos(), preg_match() or any branch that decides whether the upload proceeds. This value is a request header field — fully attacker-controlled and never validated by PHP.

rules.description: MIME prefix test on a variable that holds a client-declared type
rules.false_positive_notes: Safe if the variable came from finfo_file(), mime_content_type(), wp_get_image_mime() or wp_check_filetype_and_ext(). A finding if it was assigned from $_FILES[..]['type'] or from an aliased copy of a $_FILES element — the assignment is usually several lines above, so this regex cannot resolve it. Always read the assignment.

rules.description: wp_handle_upload()/wp_handle_sideload() with test_form disabled
rules.false_positive_notes: Downgraded to low after integration testing: this regex fired on a CORRECT upload config in tests/fixtures/safe.php. The conditions that make it a real finding are array-level, not line-level, so no single-line regex can express them and every hit needs triage by construction. test_form => false is normal and often required for AJAX/REST handlers. It is a finding only when (a) the same $overrides array has no 'mimes' key, or (b) 'test_type' => false is also present, or (c) the caller performs no capability/nonce check. Grep the matched line and the ~8 lines around it for 'mimes' and 'test_type' before triaging.

rules.description: Dangerous-extension blocklist (denylist) rather than an allowlist
rules.false_positive_notes: Matches the literal array of "banned" extensions. Every such list is incomplete by construction — .phtml, .phar, .phps, .php7, .pht, .shtml, .htaccess, .user.ini and server-specific handler extensions are routinely omitted. Also matches hardening .htaccess RemoveHandler lines, which are a *good* sign; check the file context.

rules.description: wp_check_filetype() used as the only type check (filename-only, no content sniff)
rules.false_positive_notes: wp_check_filetype() looks at the *name* only. It is acceptable as a first gate but must be paired with wp_check_filetype_and_ext() (which runs finfo/getimagesize on the actual bytes). Does not match wp_check_filetype_and_ext() because of the required '(' .

rules.description: File written from a remote/fetched body — an upload sink with no $_FILES
rules.false_positive_notes: Very noisy (caches, logs, .htaccess writers). Triage: is any part of the destination path or filename attacker-influenced (basename($url), $_POST value, a filename echoed back from a remote response), and is the destination inside a web-served directory? This is the sink that upload-focused rules miss entirely.

rules.description: Unauthenticated entry point reachable without login
rules.false_positive_notes: Not a vulnerability on its own — it is the severity multiplier. Every UPLOAD-001..007 hit that is reachable from one of these becomes a CVSS 9.8 candidate. Note that a handler hooked to a *public form processor* filter (e.g. a form plugin's "process_before" filter) is equally unauthenticated but matches neither pattern.

title: DOM-based XSS in plugin and theme JavaScript
fix_apis: Node.append() / Element.append() with a string or Text node
URL / URLSearchParams with an origin comparison

rules.description: A jQuery HTML-parsing sink (.html/.append/.prepend/.after/.before/ .replaceWith/.wrap*) is fed a string built by concatenation or a template literal with an interpolation.
rules.false_positive_notes: 49 hits per 1.07M lines of non-minified JavaScript (0.05/KLOC) across seven mature plugins. Nearly every hit is a real HTML string being assembled from runtime values; the only benign case is one where every interpolated value is provably plugin-authored (a translated constant, a loop index, a generated class name). Because these methods parse their argument as HTML, the fix is never "escape the string" - it is to build a node and set .text()/.textContent, or to escape each interpolated value with wp.escapeHtml()/_.escape() before concatenation.

rules.description: The same jQuery HTML-parsing sinks fed a bare variable or property, where the value's provenance is not visible on the line.
rules.false_positive_notes: 657 hits per 1.07M JS LOC (0.61/KLOC) - the noisiest rule here, because `.append( $node )` with an already-constructed jQuery object or DOM node is both extremely common and completely safe. Triage by asking what the argument IS: a jQuery object or an Element is safe; a string is a sink. jQuery only parses a *string* as HTML, and only when it starts with `<`. Note that `.append( someString )` where someString came from `.data()`, `JSON.parse`, an AJAX response, or a template literal assigned on an earlier line is a real finding that this rule is the only one to catch.

rules.description: Native HTML-parsing sinks - innerHTML/outerHTML assignment, insertAdjacentHTML(), document.write().
rules.false_positive_notes: 145 hits per 1.07M JS LOC (0.14/KLOC). The dominant benign shape is `el.innerHTML = ''` (a clear) and `el.innerHTML = ''`. The `[^=]` guard stops the rule matching `===` and `!==` comparisons on a property named innerHTML, which is what a naive `innerHTML\s*=` matches. Read the right-hand side: a literal is fine, anything else is a sink. Remember that innerHTML does not execute a plain `

rules.description: DOM sources - the browser-side equivalents of a superglobal. Fires on location.search/hash/href/pathname, document.URL/documentURI/referrer and URLSearchParams.
rules.false_positive_notes: 355 hits per 1.07M JS LOC (0.33/KLOC). A presence check, not a vulnerability check - these are read legitimately for routing, analytics, canonical links, "current page" highlighting and cache keys. Its value is as an inventory: list every site that touches a DOM source, then join that list against the sink rules above. A file that contains both a XSSD-004 hit and a XSSD-001/003 hit is where you start reading. Note that `location.hash` is never sent to the server, so a hash-sourced payload leaves no trace in access logs and is invisible to a WAF.

rules.description: A window "message" listener is registered. postMessage handlers receive data from ANY origin unless the handler checks event.origin itself.
rules.false_positive_notes: 32 hits per 1.07M JS LOC (0.03/KLOC). Cheap enough to read every one. The rule deliberately cannot tell a safe handler from an unsafe one, because the check that makes it safe (`if (event.origin !== expected) return;`) is usually on a different line from the registration; on the fixture the one-line safe form is reported as a hit and that is expected. Triage is a three-line read of the callback body: (1) is event.origin compared against an allow-list? (2) is event.source compared against the frame you created? (3) does the payload reach a sink? Missing (1) plus present (3) is a finding regardless of what the payload looks like.

rules.description: A navigation sink - window.open(), location.href/assign/replace - is given a variable rather than a literal. A `javascript:` URL here is script execution, not a redirect.
rules.false_positive_notes: 111 hits per 1.07M JS LOC (0.10/KLOC). Benign when the variable was built from a same-origin base (`new URL(path, location.origin)`) or came from a server-rendered admin_url(). A finding when the value traces to a DOM source, a data attribute, a postMessage payload, or an AJAX response. The control is a scheme allow-list - `/^https?:\/\//` or a same-origin URL comparison - not escaping; there is no escaper that makes `javascript:` safe.

rules.description: Triple-brace interpolation in a wp.template / Underscore template. In WordPress's template settings `{{{ }}}` is the UNESCAPED interpolation and `{{ }}` is the escaped one, so every triple brace is a raw HTML write.
rules.false_positive_notes: 385 hits per 1.47M lines of PHP (0.26/KLOC) - templates live inside PHP files as often as in .html ones, so run this over both. Every hit is genuinely an unescaped write; whether it is a vulnerability depends entirely on whether the interpolated member is user-controlled. Values that are plugin-generated URLs, enum-like status strings or pre-escaped `*_html` members are fine. Values that trace to a display name, a title, a caption or any editable setting are not. Beware the near-miss: `{{{ }}}` and `{{ }}` differ by one character and are routinely mixed within a single template - see CVE-2024-2123.

rules.description: Server-to-client data channel built from PHP variables - wp_add_inline_script() or wp_localize_script() whose payload is not a literal.
rules.false_positive_notes: 24 hits per 1.47M LOC of PHP (0.02/KLOC). Neither function is itself an XSS sink - wp_localize_script() JSON-encodes with JSON_HEX_TAG, which protects the surrounding script block - so a hit is not a finding on its own. It is a handoff: the value crosses into JavaScript here, and the question moves to what the JavaScript does with it. Two things make this worth flagging anyway. First, WP_Scripts::localize() runs html_entity_decode( (string) $value, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8' ) over every SCALAR value, so any esc_html()/esc_attr() applied first is silently undone (non-scalar members are skipped by that loop and pass through untouched). Second, wp_add_inline_script() does NOT JSON-encode anything - it emits your string verbatim into the script block, so a `</script>` in an interpolated value ends the block.

rules.description: A value is read back out of an HTML data attribute with .data() or .attr('data-...') - the standard channel by which contributor-stored settings reach page-builder JavaScript.
rules.false_positive_notes: 811 hits per 1.07M JS LOC (0.76/KLOC), the highest rate in this file, because reading a data attribute is ordinary and usually harmless. It is included because in the WordPress ecosystem this is the dominant STORED DOM-XSS channel - the plugin escapes the value correctly with esc_attr() on the way into the attribute, and the escaping is irrelevant once the browser hands the decoded string back to jQuery. Treat it as the second half of a join: a file with both a XSSD-009 hit and a XSSD-001/002/003 hit deserves a read. Note that .data() auto-parses JSON, so a data attribute can deliver a whole object graph, and that base64 or JSON layering (CVE-2025-8451) hides markup from every attribute-level review.

title: Reflected XSS via request data echoed without context-correct escaping

rules.description: echo/print of a superglobal directly, with no escaping wrapper
rules.false_positive_notes: Zero hits across 256k LOC of five mature audited plugins, so a hit is almost always real. The only benign shapes are echoing a value the caller already hardened (rare, because the superglobal is being read inline here) and echoing into a context where the payload cannot execute (a comment, a Content-Type that is not HTML). Confirm the output context before deciding which escaper to recommend - do not assume esc_html.

rules.description: Short echo tag printing a superglobal
rules.false_positive_notes: Same profile as XSSR-001. `<?=` is always an echo, so there is no wrapper. Note that short_open_tag is irrelevant - `<?=` is always available since PHP 5.4.

rules.description: echo/print of a bare variable that is not wrapped in any function call (the token right after the echo keyword is `$`, not an identifier)
rules.false_positive_notes: 203 hits per 256k LOC (0.79/KLOC) versus 3489 for a naive "echo with a variable" pattern - a 94% noise reduction, but the residue is real and must be triaged. Dominant benign case: the value was escaped on a previous line and stored (`$safe = esc_html($x); echo $safe;`), which the WordPress docs explicitly sanction when the variable is suffixed `_escaped`, `_safe` or `_clean`. Second benign case: the value is a constant, an integer counter, or plugin-authored markup. Triage rule for a reviewing agent - walk back to the assignment of that variable; if the assignment is a literal, a cast, or an esc_*/wp_kses* call, drop it; if the assignment traces to $_GET/$_POST/ $_REQUEST/$_SERVER/$_COOKIE or to a database read, keep it and then judge the output context.

rules.description: Output of add_query_arg()/remove_query_arg() with no escaping wrapper - these default to $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'] when no URL argument is supplied
rules.false_positive_notes: 0 hits across the 256k LOC negative corpus, while `esc_url( add_query_arg( ... ) )` appeared 48 times in the same corpus - the correct form is what maintained code actually contains, so the bare form stands out cleanly. Do NOT add `return` to the keyword alternation - `return add_query_arg(...)` is a transport, not an output sink, and adding it took this rule from 0 hits to 47 on the same corpus. Flag only at the point of emission.

rules.description: Superglobal concatenated into a string that is being built as markup
rules.false_positive_notes: 10 hits per 256k LOC. Fires on string building regardless of whether the string is ever echoed - a value concatenated into a log line, a SQL string, or an HTTP header is not reflected XSS (though it may well be another class). Check what happens to the assembled variable.

rules.description: Use of the server variables that carry attacker-controlled request text - REQUEST_URI, PHP_SELF, QUERY_STRING, HTTP_REFERER
rules.false_positive_notes: A presence check, not a vulnerability check. These variables are legitimately read for routing, caching keys, canonical URLs and nonce actions. Its value is as an inventory - enumerate every site that touches them, then check each one for an output path. Modern browsers percent-encode the path portion of REQUEST_URI, which is why several CVEs in this family carry the NVD qualifier "in old web browsers"; the query string, and PHP_SELF under PATH_INFO-style server configs, are not encoded, so treat the qualifier as narrowing severity, not eliminating it.

rules.description: printf/vprintf whose first argument variable is passed unescaped
rules.false_positive_notes: 22 hits per 256k LOC, most of them benign because the corresponding format specifier is numeric (`%d`, `%u`) and therefore casts the argument. Read the format string - only `%s` positions matter. This rule exists because printf output is invisible to every echo-anchored rule, and at least one real CVE in this class emitted its payload through `printf('%s', $url)`.

rules.description: Inline PHP echo of a bare variable or superglobal directly inside a quoted HTML attribute value
rules.false_positive_notes: 49 hits per 256k LOC. Precise because `value="<?php echo esc_attr($x); ?>"` does not match - the token after `echo` is an identifier, not `$`. Every hit is an attribute-context output with no wrapper, so the correct fix is nearly always esc_attr(), or esc_url() when the attribute is href/src/action/formaction. Residual noise is the same "escaped on an earlier line" case as XSSR-003.

rules.description: Double-quoted PHP string with variable interpolation being echoed, where the string contains an HTML attribute assignment
rules.false_positive_notes: Interpolation hides the value from every wrapper-anchored rule because there is no function call to look for. Benign when the interpolated variable is an integer, a plugin constant, or an already-escaped variable. Heredoc bodies use the same interpolation and are NOT matched by this rule - grep separately for `<<<` if the codebase uses them.

title: Stored XSS via saved content re-emitted without context-correct escaping

rules.description: An HTML attribute value is opened with a quote, the PHP string literal is closed, and a bare variable is concatenated in - the canonical attribute break-out shape (`class="' . $x . '"`).
rules.false_positive_notes: 968 hits per 1.47M LOC (0.66/KLOC) on the negative corpus, versus 4757 for a naive "echo with a variable" sweep - a 80% noise reduction that keeps every fixture true positive. It fires on string *building* regardless of whether the result is ever emitted, and it cannot see an escaper applied on an earlier line. The residue is dominated by two benign shapes: (a) the value is a plugin constant, an integer, or a hard-coded URL, and (b) the value was escaped at its assignment. Note the rule is deliberately blind to the wrapper - it only asks "was the token after the concatenation dot a `$`?" - because `. esc_attr( $x )` has an identifier there and never matches. That is what keeps it cheap and lookahead-free.

rules.description: Same break-out shape, but the attribute is one that takes a URL, so the fix is esc_url() and not esc_attr().
rules.false_positive_notes: 26 hits per 1.47M LOC (0.02/KLOC). Nearly every hit is a real missing esc_url(). The benign residue is a hard-coded vendor URL held in a variable, or a URL that already went through esc_url()/sanitize_url() at assignment. Treat a hit as a finding until you have walked back to the assignment. Distinguish this from XSSS-001 because `esc_attr()` is NOT a valid fix here - it passes `javascript:` through untouched.

rules.description: A PHP variable is interpolated inside a double-quoted string that is building an HTML attribute (`"<div class=\"{$atts['cls']}\">"`). No function call exists, so every wrapper-anchored rule is blind to it.
rules.false_positive_notes: 584 hits per 1.47M LOC (0.40/KLOC). Interpolation is the main way an attribute sink hides from concatenation-based rules, which is why this rule exists despite the noise. Benign cases are numeric ids, loop counters, generated CSS class prefixes, and values already hardened at assignment. Heredoc and nowdoc bodies use the same `{$var}` syntax and are matched by this rule only when the attribute assignment and the interpolation land on one line - grep `<<<` separately and read those bodies by hand.

rules.description: A persistent-storage read is echoed with no wrapper at all - the shortest possible stored-XSS statement.
rules.false_positive_notes: 1 hit per 1.47M LOC of mature audited code, and that one hit is `echo get_option( 'blog_charset' )` - a core option with a constrained value set. In other words this rule is silent on well-maintained code, so a hit in an unaudited plugin is almost certainly real. Confirm the output context before naming the fix: a meta value landing in `href` needs esc_url(), not esc_html().

rules.description: A shortcode / block / widget attribute array element is concatenated or interpolated directly, with no escaping wrapper. This is the single most common contributor-reachable stored-XSS shape in the ecosystem.
rules.false_positive_notes: 14 hits per 1.47M LOC (0.01/KLOC). Very quiet because the correct forms (`esc_attr( $atts['x'] )`, `$atts['x'],` as a function argument) put a `)` or a `,` after the closing bracket rather than a `.` or a `}`. Residual noise is string building that never reaches markup - building a cache key, a CSS file path, an option name. The variable names are a heuristic: rename-happy codebases use `$a`, `$args`, `$params`, `$props`; widen the alternation to match the local convention before trusting a zero-hit result.

rules.description: A value is run through an entity DECODER. Whatever escaping the storage layer or KSES left in place is undone at this point, and everything downstream is raw again.
rules.false_positive_notes: 95 hits per 1.47M LOC (0.06/KLOC). Cheap enough to read every hit. Legitimate uses exist - decoding before a strlen()/mb_strlen() width calculation, before a strict string comparison, or before writing to a plain-text email body or a PDF. The rule earns its place because when the decoded value then reaches markup, it is a guaranteed XSS with no escaping anywhere in the chain (this is CVE-2023-7070 exactly). Triage question: does the decoded value reach an echo/return that produces HTML?

rules.description: An escaping function is wrapped around the printf/sprintf FORMAT STRING while an argument is passed bare. The format string is usually a translated constant, so the escaping protects nothing and the untrusted argument is interpolated raw.
rules.false_positive_notes: 60 hits per 1.47M LOC (0.04/KLOC). A hit is benign when the bare argument is an integer, is bound to a `%d`/`%u` specifier, or was escaped at assignment. Read the format string: only `%s` positions matter. This mistake is particularly hard to spot in review because the line visibly contains an `esc_*` call, which satisfies a "did they escape it?" skim - see CVE-2023-1404.

rules.description: A superglobal is written straight into persistent storage with no sanitizer. This is the input half of the class: it does not itself prove an XSS, but it guarantees that every reader of that key is unprotected.
rules.false_positive_notes: 0 hits per 1.47M LOC. Mature code always interposes a sanitizer or a cast, so any hit is an unreviewed write path. Remember that clearing this rule is not sufficient: sanitizing on input does not license echoing on output, and sanitize_text_field() in particular leaves `"` and `'` intact.

rules.description: A variable is used as the REPLACEMENT argument of preg_replace/str_replace. The replacement is spliced into the subject with no escaping, so if the subject is markup this is an output sink that no echo-anchored rule can see.
rules.false_positive_notes: 82 hits per 1.47M LOC (0.06/KLOC), most of them benign because the subject is a file path, a SQL fragment, a slug, or a plain-text string rather than markup. The rule exists because CVE-2024-0255 is invisible to every other rule in this file: the sink is `preg_replace( '/#[0-9a-f]{3,6}/mi', $color, $icon )` where `$icon` is SVG markup. Triage by asking what the SUBJECT is, not what the replacement is. Note that with preg_replace a `$` or `\\` in the replacement is also a backreference, so untrusted replacements have a second failure mode.

title: XML external entity injection and unsafe XML parsing

rules.description: An explicitly dangerous libxml flag passed to a parser. LIBXML_NOENT turns entity substitution back ON, and LIBXML_DTDLOAD makes the parser fetch the external DTD subset. Since libxml 2.9.0 both are off by default, so their presence is a deliberate opt-in to the vulnerable behaviour.
rules.false_positive_notes: The flag is safe only when paired with a working external-entity block for the PHP version in use, and on PHP 8 no such block exists any more (libxml_disable_entity_loader() is a no-op). Treat LIBXML_NOENT on modern PHP as a finding by default. Note the rule deliberately does not match the benign constants LIBXML_NOCDATA, LIBXML_NOBLANKS or LIBXML_NONET, which look similar in review and are frequently confused with these two.

rules.description: Any call to libxml_disable_entity_loader(). Both arguments are findings for different reasons - (false) re-enables external entity loading process-wide, and (true) is deprecated and has no effect from PHP 8.0, so code relying on it for protection is unprotected on modern PHP.
rules.false_positive_notes: A (true) call is harmless in itself on PHP 8; the finding is whatever it was protecting. Always read the parse call it wraps and check for LIBXML_NOENT. A version gate around the call (`if ( PHP_VERSION_ID < 80000 )`) is a specific and serious anti-pattern - see the WordPress core case study - because it removes the guard on exactly the versions where the developer assumed it was unnecessary.

rules.description: DOMDocument construction and its load family (load, loadXML, loadHTMLFile). DOMDocument is safe by default on current libxml but is the most common carrier for an explicit LIBXML_NOENT.
rules.false_positive_notes: Reclassified low by scripts/test_rules.py: this fires on correct code in tests/fixtures/safe.php, and kb/SCHEMA.md reserves high/medium for rules that stay silent there. No coverage is lost - the high-confidence rules in this class still cover the unambiguous shapes; this one is the worklist that needs triage. The correctly hardened form also matches - `$dom->resolveExternals = false; $dom->substituteEntities = false; $dom->load( $f, LIBXML_NONET );` produces two hits and is fine. Triage by reading the flags argument and the two properties. `->load(` is a generic method name and will also match unrelated loaders (`$config->load()`, `$template->load()`); confirm the receiver is a DOM object.

rules.description: The SimpleXML family - simplexml_load_string(), simplexml_load_file() and new SimpleXMLElement(). The third argument of the load functions is the flags argument that carries LIBXML_NOENT.
rules.false_positive_notes: A default-flag call is safe on PHP 8 and on any PHP built against libxml 2.9.0 or later with the entity loader left alone. It is not safe on PHP 7 in a process where anything has called libxml_disable_entity_loader( false ), which is why the calls still need to be enumerated. Priority order for reading hits - those with a third argument first, then those parsing an uploaded or fetched document, then the rest.

rules.description: A request superglobal reaching an XML parser directly, optionally through one or two wrapping calls such as file_get_contents(), wp_unslash() or stripslashes().
rules.false_positive_notes: Essentially none as a finding of "untrusted XML is parsed here". Whether it is exploitable still depends on the PHP/libxml version and the flags, so record the PHP version constraint in the report rather than dropping the finding.

rules.description: The property form of the same opt-in - DOMDocument::$substituteEntities or ::$resolveExternals set to true. Equivalent to LIBXML_NOENT / LIBXML_DTDLOAD but contains none of those tokens.
rules.false_positive_notes: Very low volume. The only benign reason to set substituteEntities = true is a document with internal entity definitions the code genuinely needs expanded, which still requires the external loader to be blocked separately. The `= false` form is the hardening and is deliberately not matched.

rules.description: Legacy and streaming XML parsers - the expat wrappers xml_parser_create()/xml_parse(), and XMLReader. Different API surface, same entity semantics, and none of the other rules see them.
rules.false_positive_notes: expat does not expand external entities at all, so xml_parser_create() hits are usually informational - but they mark a file that consumes untrusted XML, which is exactly where the *other* parsers in the same file matter. XMLReader needs LIBXML_NOENT (or ::setParserProperty with SUBST_ENTITIES) to be dangerous; check for those on any XMLReader hit.

rules.description: SVG upload surface. An SVG is an XML document, so a plugin that whitelists the SVG MIME type or branches on image/svg+xml has created an author-level channel for attacker-authored XML - the entry point for the majority of recent WordPress XXE reports.
rules.false_positive_notes: Not a vulnerability on its own; it is a *reachability* rule. Many hits are icon pickers, MIME allowlists or front-end sprite handling with no parser anywhere. Its value is correlation - an XXE-008 hit in a codebase that also has XXE-003 or XXE-004 hits means untrusted XML almost certainly reaches a parser. Also matches `upload_mimes` filters that have nothing to do with SVG; read the callback.
